entry.title: Coast Guard suspends search for missing paddleboarder off Jupiter Inlet
entry.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard has suspended its search for missing paddleboarder Matt Pawlowski, 48, who was last seen off Jupiter Inlet, pending new information. 'The decision to suspend an active search is one of the most difficult decisions we make, and it comes only after every reasonable effort to locate the missing person has been exhausted,' Captain Frank Florio, commander of Coast Guard Sector Miami, said. 'Our crews and partner agencies searched tirelessly for Matt. I am deeply grateful to everyone who answered the call and supported this extensive search. Our hearts are with Matt's family, friends, and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,' Florio said. Pawlowski was last seen Sept. 15 at approximately 9 a.m. heading east approximately 4 miles off Jupiter Beach aboard a 14-foot lime-green and yellow paddleboard. He was reportedly wearing a white hat, orange shirt and gray shorts. A Good Samaritan located a paddleboard matching the description of the one Pawlowski was using approximately 10 miles offshore Jupiter Island on Sept. 16. The paddleboard was returned to local law enforcement. Over the course of the multi-day search, Coast Guard air and surface crews conducted extensive nighttime and daytime operations. Assets involved included Coast Guard Cutters Margaret Norvell, Robert Yered, Pablo Valent and Skipjack, along with HC-130 aircraft from Air Station Elizabeth City and Air Station Miami, and Station Lake Worth Inlet and Station Fort Pierce. U.S. Space Force also assisted in identifying search areas. Search efforts were based on Pawlowski's last-known position, drift patterns and possible routes. Anyone with information that may assist search efforts is asked to contact Coast Guard Sector Miami at 305-535-4472.

entry.title: Former NYPD officer who worked Ground Zero now leads Martin County school safety - WPTV
entry.summary: Former NYPD officer who worked Ground Zero now leads Martin County school safety    WPTV
entry.article_text: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. "There are thousands upon thousands of stories. This is just mine," he said. "Everybody says that time heals all, and I know for me and everybody who was down there -- we're still waiting."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: Florida governor signs death warrant for William Reaves Jr., convicted of killing Indian River County deputy    WPTV
entry.article_text: Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20, at 6 p.m.WATCH BELOW: Man who killed Indian River Co. deputy to be executed in OctoberReaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store.Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves's shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face.As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, "I wouldn't do that if I were you." The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times.Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach.The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994.Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades.In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied.Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that "the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant," and confirmed that "there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause."The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman accused of elder exploitation, including draining $100K from accounts - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman accused of elder exploitation, including draining $100K from accounts    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 60-year-old woman was arrested after an investigation by the Port St. Lucie Police Department in alleged exploitation and neglect of an elderly and medically vulnerable man. Barbara Baumgarten is accused of draining around $100,000 from the 85-year-old man's bank accounts and listed herself as a co-borrower on a $616,550 mortgage. She is facing felony charges of grand theft from a person 65 years of age or older, exploitation of an elderly person or disabled adult and neglect of an elderly person or disabled adult. Baumgarten was arrested with help from the U.S. On Thursday, she was booked at the St. Lucie County Jail and remains there on $310,000 bond. Her first appearance was Friday. This investigation began on March 18, when an elderly man was found injured on the floor of his Port St. Lucie home by Baumgarten, his caregiver. The victim initially reported that four men had entered his home and assaulted him. Surveillance footage showed no one entering or leaving the property, and no signs of forced entry or theft. He provided inconsistent accounts of what occurred. Detectives determined the victim was experiencing significant cognitive issues. But detectives continued looking into the victim’s overall well-being and circumstances. The investigation shifted toward concerns of elder exploitation and neglect, and grew into the months-long investigation documented in a 45-page investigative report. As the victim’s physical and cognitive health declined, he became increasingly dependent on Baumgarten, investigators found. They determined that Baumgarten had assumed significant control over the victim’s finances and legal affairs, including power of attorney and healthcare surrogate. Detectives also learned the victim had been isolated from family and friends, and that changes had been made to his estate documents that benefited Baumgarten. Records reviewed by detectives showed there was a decline in his financial accounts from $105,971 in March 2023 to approximately $4,897 by April 2026 . Investigators also uncovered a $616,550 mortgage on Baumgarten’s residence in which the victim was listed as a co-borrower. That is despite the property being solely in Baumgarten’s name and evidence that the victim was reportedly unaware his signature appeared on the mortgage. Detectives worked with healthcare providers, caregivers, family members, financial institutions and other agencies to establish the full extent of the circumstances surrounding the victim’s care and finances. The Florida Department of Children and Families ultimately substantiated allegations of exploitation and determined that the victim lacked the capacity to independently make his own decisions. The victim was removed from Baumgarten’s care, placed under a temporary guardianship, and reunited with his family. "This case serves as a reminder of the importance of looking beyond the initial circumstances when something does not appear right," the police agency said in a news release. "Through an extensive investigation, detectives were able to uncover concerns involving the care, finances, and well-being of a vulnerable member of our community and ultimately help ensure his safety. entry.title: 'Just heard like two big pop pops': Two men arrested after road rage shooting in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Just heard like two big pop pops': Two men arrested after road rage shooting in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: Two men were arrested after a road rage incident escalated into a shooting near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace. Neighbors reported hearing gunfire at approximately 6:30 p.m. "OK, last night we were trying to put the kids down, and we just heard like two big pop pops," resident Ripley Crawford said. "All we saw was the cars were kind of already pulled to the side, and you could see there was like a crash of sorts." The Port St. Lucie Police Department determined the incident stemmed from a misunderstanding between two drivers following a lane change and merging near Southwest Crosstown Parkway. One driver believed he was being followed after the vehicles crossed paths, but investigators found no intentional following. One of the drivers, 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. The other driver, 41-year-old Dean Plotts, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office deputy traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Later that night, traffic was rerouted as investigators gathered evidence at the scene. "The traffic was just nonstop because they closed California. My neighbor got a call from her daughter in Tennessee that said there was a shooting down here," resident Ernie Lampreda said. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Detectives responded to the scene and collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, and dash cam footage that captured portions of the incident. Based on the evidence, witness information, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody, and the investigation remains ongoing. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.summary: A West Palm Beach woman has been arrested on DUI and vehicular homicide charges following a wrong-way crash that ultimately killed another driver, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office (PBSO). Fany M. Rosa, 36, was arrested and booked into the Palm Beach County jail on Sept. 18 in connection with the Aug. 23 crash on the Southern Boulevard overpass at Jog Road, according to PBSO. Investigators said Rosa was driving a 2017 Toyota Corolla eastbound in the westbound lanes of Southern Boulevard around 6:06 a.m. when she collided with a 2019 Honda Insight traveling westbound near the top of the Jog Road overpass. Both drivers suffered critical, life-threatening injuries and were taken to a hospital. Toxicology testing for Rosa was pending at the time of the initial investigation. The Honda's driver, Corey Watson, 36, of Lantana, died on Aug. 29 from injuries sustained in the crash, according to an updated PBSO report. Rosa now faces charges of vehicular homicide, DUI causing death, DUI causing property damage and reckless driving causing property damage, according to PBSO. The investigation remains ongoing.

entry.article_text: Lucie road rage incident that escalated into a physical fight and shooting landed two men in handcuffs Thursday. Lucie Police Department, the incident happened at about 6:30 p.m. near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace. Police said that before the shooting, one driver believed he was being followed after merging onto Southwest Crosstown Parkway. The vehicles had passed each other, and one driver believed the other had cut him off. Investigators determined there was no intentional following, police said. One of the drivers, identified as Tylon Kukielka, 57, was driving with his girlfriend to her home after leaving a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as Dean Plotts, 41, was traveling in the same direction. Police said the situation escalated into a physical fight near Southwest Brevity Terrace. During the fight, Kukielka allegedly fired his gun, striking Plotts twice in the left wrist and legs. See also: Formerly conjoined twins see each other face-to-face after historic separation surgery A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy traveling in the area witnessed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also taken to a hospital for a medical evaluation. Investigators recovered surveillance video and shell casings during the investigation. Detectives later charged Kukielka with attempted homicide. Plotts was charged with burglary with assault or battery. Both men were taken into custody. The incident remains under investigation.

entry.article_text: 38-year-old Darrel Abbey is facing multiple charges after Martin County deputies say he barricaded himself inside a Palm City guest house during an hours-long standoff with law enforcement Saturday . According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Abbey was taken into custody after SWAT officers and hostage negotiators spent hours trying to convince him to surrender. Deputies said they were initially called to a home along SW Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road for a domestic-related incident. Investigators say the situation escalated when Abbey, who deputies say was armed and dangerous and under the influence of alcohol, barricaded himself inside a guest house on the property. "I was pretty scared because it doesn't usually happen in our neighborhood," said 11-year-old Gavin Ryan, who lives next door. See also: Routine warrant leads to shocking major animal cruelty bust in Lake Worth Ryan's mother said deputies asked her to evacuate after she heard several gunshots coming from her neighbor's yard. SWAT officers later positioned themselves near her home as the standoff unfolded. Deputies said hostage negotiators worked throughout the afternoon to get Abbey to come out peacefully. He eventually surrendered without incident and no injuries were reported. Another neighbor, Julian Tracy, said he was shocked to learn what was happening. "[Gavin's] mom told me about it, and I was like, 'Whoa,' Tracy said. "I've never heard about a shooting in someone's neighborhood." Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail and is facing three charges, including felony aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Jail records show he is being held on a $12,500 bond.

entry.article_text: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operationOperation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday.Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement."Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said.The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said.During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online."Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked."We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said.Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County."We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said.FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county."This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said.Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors."Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today."FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. entry.title: Tropical Storm Fay strengthens in the far eastern Atlantic
entry.summary: Tropical Storm Fay formed in the Atlantic Ocean Sunday morning as the system strengthened hundreds of miles southwest of the Azores. As of the 5 p.m. EDT advisory, Fay had maximum sustained winds of 65 mph and was located about 430 miles southwest of the Azores. The storm was moving north-northeast at 6 mph. Fay is a compact storm, with tropical-storm-force winds extending up to about 45 miles from its center. The storm is expected to continue moving generally north-northeast for about another day before turning toward the southwest Monday as a ridge builds to its north. Fay's opportunity to strengthen is expected to be short-lived. Increasing wind shear and dry air are forecast to cause the storm to weaken beginning Monday. The National Hurricane Center forecasts Fay to become a post-tropical remnant low by Tuesday and dissipate by the end of the week. There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect, and the storm currently poses no hazards to land. entry.title: 18 suspects accused in the July 2021 killing of Haiti's president being extradited from Haiti to US
entry.summary: Eighteen suspects who were arrested in the July 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Mose were awaiting extradition to the U.S. on Sunday, marking the end of a drawn-out judicial process in Haiti for a killing that shocked the troubled Caribbean country. The suspects will face trial in Florida, according to Jason Reding Quiones, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida. Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination of President Jovenel Mose, he wrote on X. We will follow the evidence wherever it leads, to those who financed it, facilitated it, supported it or committed crimes to make it possible. Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished. Quiones did not identify the suspects, and a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday. The suspects who remain in Haiti awaiting trial included more than a dozen Colombian soldiers, a former Haitian police officer and Joseph Badio, a former Haiti Ministry of Justice employee who was part of an anti-corruption unit. Badio, considered a key suspect, was arrested in Haiti in October 2023 after being on the run for more than two years. Families of suspects surprised by extradition Quiones said that 30 people have been indicted in Moses killing, with FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles noting that there were multiple arrests in the U.S. and abroad on Sunday. He said that the FBI and others remain steadfast in ensuring that all individuals who allegedly sought profit from the assassination of a head of state are held fully accountable. The wife of one of the suspects, Diana Marcela Arbelez Llano, said in a phone interview Sunday from Colombia that the extradition caught her and the relatives of the other suspects by surprise. We never imagined that the United States would have take them so suddenly, she said, adding that she hopes they have the opportunity to prove their innocence. Arbelez said all the detained Colombians are very sick given the notoriously inhumane conditions in Haitian prisons, and that while she hopes their health will improve in the U.S., she remains worried. I dont know why the United States would have taken them, she said. Its a state of total uncertainty. Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished.”Quiñones did not identify the suspects, and a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday.The suspects who remain in Haiti awaiting trial included more than a dozen Colombian soldiers, a former Haitian police officer and Joseph Badio, a former Haiti Ministry of Justice employee who was part of an anti-corruption unit. Badio, considered a key suspect, was arrested in Haiti in October 2023 after being on the run for more than two years.Families of suspects surprised by extraditionQuiñones said that 30 people have been indicted in Moïse’s killing, with FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles noting that there were multiple arrests in the U.S. and abroad on Sunday.He said that the FBI and others “remain steadfast in ensuring that all individuals who allegedly sought profit from the assassination of a head of state are held fully accountable.”The wife of one of the suspects, Diana Marcela Arbeláez Llano, said in a phone interview Sunday from Colombia that the extradition caught her and the relatives of the other suspects by surprise.“We never imagined that the United States would have take them so suddenly,” she said, adding that she hopes they have the opportunity to prove their innocence.Arbeláez said all the detained Colombians are very sick given the notoriously inhumane conditions in Haitian prisons, and that while she hopes their health will improve in the U.S., she remains worried.“I don’t know why the United States would have taken them,” she said. “It’s a state of total uncertainty.”Relatives of the Colombian suspects had previously complained about the repeated delays in the Haitian judicial process following their arrest in 2021, with the investigation stalled by gang violence, death threats and a crumbling judicial system.In October 2025, justice officials in Haiti asked the U.S. and Canada for help after a local court of appeals ordered a new investigation into Moïse's killing, the third inquiry of its kind since he was fatally shot at his private residence in July 2021. The previous investigations were stalled because Haitian judges kept resigning from the case, fearing for their lives, and gangs seized control of the downtown Port-au-Prince courthouse where the judges were interrogating suspects.US pushes forward with prosecutionsThe extradition comes as the U.S. continues to prosecute and sentence multiple other suspects in the case.In May, a jury in Florida convicted four men in the killing, and at least five others have pleaded guilty and are serving life sentences.Those recently convicted include Arcángel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages, all of whom pleaded not guilty. A jury found them guilty of conspiring to kill or kidnap Haiti’s elected leader and providing material support for the plot.Still awaiting trial is Christian Sanon, a Haitian-American citizen whom authorities said was initially picked by the alleged conspirators to replace Moïse. Once in power, the plan was for him to award contracts to a company known as CTU for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment.Ortiz and Intriago were principals for CTU, which stood for Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security. Meanwhile, Veintemilla was a principal of Worldwide Capital Lending Group. Both companies were based in South Florida.Suspects who previously pleaded guilty in U.S. federal court include a retired Colombian army officer and a Haitian-Chilean businessman who was once an informant for the U.S. government.Authorities said that key fugitives in the case include Dimitri Hérard, ex-head of security at Haiti’s National Palace, who escaped last year after a powerful gang federation stormed Haiti’s two biggest prisons.

entry.title: Wet, stormy pattern holds through the week for the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: Wet, stormy pattern holds through the week for the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast are heading into another humid, unsettled stretch, with daily showers and thunderstorms remaining in the forecast through much of the upcoming week. The biggest weather concern will be not simply the number of storms, but the potential for slow-moving or repeatedly developing downpours that can quickly overwhelm poor-drainage and urban areas. An upper-level low near the northeast Gulf Coast is helping hold plenty of tropical moisture over South Florida this weekend. Moisture in the atmosphere remains unusually high, setting the stage for scattered to numerous showers and storms, especially during the afternoon and early evening. For Sunday and Monday, weak steering winds mean storms may move slowly at times. The greatest coverage should develop over the interior and east-coast metro areas, including Palm Beach County, after the sea breeze moves inland. A few showers could move in from the Atlantic during the morning, while storms may shift back toward the coast and offshore waters after sunset. Not every neighborhood will see flooding, but any stronger storm can produce torrential rain in a short time. Forecast guidance suggests many locations could pick up around one-half inch to an inch of rain on a given day; however, isolated locations could receive 3 to 5 inches in as little as six hours. That creates a localized flooding concern, particularly on roads, in low-lying neighborhoods and where drainage is poor. Lightning and gusty winds will remain additional storm hazards. Cooler air several miles above the ground may allow a few storms to become stronger, producing frequent lightning, wind gusts near 45 to 50 mph and, mainly north along the Treasure Coast, a small hail risk. High temperatures will generally stay in the upper 80s to near 90 degrees, while sticky humidity keeps afternoon heat indices in the 90s. The upper-level low should gradually weaken and become absorbed into the broader weather pattern early to midweek. That alone will not immediately shut off the rain. Deep moisture is expected to linger through Wednesday, keeping rain and storm chances elevated each day. Attention then turns to a frontal boundary expected to slide south through Florida sometime Friday into Saturday. There is still uncertainty in exactly how quickly the front moves and how much drier air follows it. For now, plan on daily rain opportunities and keep an eye on the forecast especially if you live or travel through flood-prone locations. Rainfall totals could add up to 5 to 7 inches in some spots over the next seven days, although those amounts will vary sharply from neighborhood to neighborhood.

entry.title: ‘You Are Not Alone’: PSL woman turns grief into community for others
entry.summary: Losing someone you love can change everything. For Stacey Comer, that loss came in 2018 when her husband, Chris, died following complications from a kidney transplant. WATCH You Are Not Alone: PSL woman turns grief into community for others You Are Not Alone: PSL woman turns grief into community for others As she learned to navigate life without him, Comer also began to notice there wasn't one central place on the Treasure Coast where people experiencing grief could go to find support, resources and connection. She started asking herself a simple question: Why isn't there an entity where all of this lives under? That question became the foundation for Chriss Place , a free, in-person grief support community Comer is now creating on the Treasure Coast. Comer said grief can be difficult to understand until you experience it yourself. She added that while friends and family often want to help, people who are grieving can still feel isolated. You only sort of know it if you're in the club, and when you're in the club everyone wants to be so supportive and helpful, Comer said. Chriss Place is intended to give people a place to connect with others who understand what they're going through. The community is not limited to people who have lost a spouse or immediate family member. Comer wants it to be available to anyone who has experienced a loss and needs support navigating what comes next. Right now, Comer is creating Chriss Place from the ground up. Her long-term vision is to create a physical space on the Treasure Coast somewhere that feels comfortable and welcoming, where people can gather, find resources and connect with others who understand grief. You are not alone. You feel alone because you think you're the only one feeling it, but you're not, Comer said. For Comer, Chriss Place is rooted in the loss of her husband but she hopes it can become something much bigger. She wants other people on the Treasure Coast to have the kind of support she realized was missing during her own journey through grief. The ultimate goal is to create a community where people don't have to navigate that journey by themselves. While grief may look different for everyone, Comer wants people to know one thing: They don't have to face it alone. For more information on the next free community grief meet-up, visit their website .

entry.summary: MCSO: Palm City man fired gun while under the influence of alcohol before SWAT standoff    cw34.com
entry.article_text: 38-year-old Darrel Abbey is facing multiple charges after Martin County deputies say he barricaded himself inside a Palm City guest house during an hours-long standoff with law enforcement Saturday . According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Abbey was taken into custody after SWAT officers and hostage negotiators spent hours trying to convince him to surrender. Deputies said they were initially called to a home along SW Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road for a domestic-related incident. Investigators say the situation escalated when Abbey, who deputies say was armed and dangerous and under the influence of alcohol, barricaded himself inside a guest house on the property. "I was pretty scared because it doesn't usually happen in our neighborhood," said 11-year-old Gavin Ryan, who lives next door. See also: Routine warrant leads to shocking major animal cruelty bust in Lake Worth Ryan's mother said deputies asked her to evacuate after she heard several gunshots coming from her neighbor's yard. SWAT officers later positioned themselves near her home as the standoff unfolded. Deputies said hostage negotiators worked throughout the afternoon to get Abbey to come out peacefully. He eventually surrendered without incident and no injuries were reported. Another neighbor, Julian Tracy, said he was shocked to learn what was happening. "[Gavin's] mom told me about it, and I was like, 'Whoa,' Tracy said. "I've never heard about a shooting in someone's neighborhood." Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail and is facing three charges, including felony aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Jail records show he is being held on a $12,500 bond.

entry.title: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? - WPEC
entry.summary: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law?    WPEC
entry.article_text: A proposed luxury waterfront development in Fort Pierce is drawing renewed attention after city commissioners approved a motion to explore hiring outside legal counsel to review whether the city has any options to challenge the project under Florida's Live Local Act. 14 vote comes as cities across Florida continue testing the limits of the state's Live Local Act and lawmakers implement the latest round of changes to the law. The proposed Causeway Cove development on South Hutchinson Island has become one of the Treasure Coast's most closely watched growth disputes, putting residents and local officials at odds with a state law that limits how much control cities have over certain housing projects. 14 meeting, the commission approved a motion to explore hiring an outside land-use attorney to determine whether Fort Pierce has any legal grounds to challenge the project under the Live Local Act. The city is also monitoring lawsuits filed elsewhere in Florida that seek to restore greater local control over development decisions. The move comes as Florida enters the latest phase of the law. Known as Live Local 4.0, the most recent changes took effect July 1, 2026, expanding eligible development sites and further clarifying protections for qualifying projects that include affordable housing. Qualifying developments must continue to reserve at least 40% of units as affordable rental housing for at least 30 years. Now, Fort Pierce finds itself at the center of a broader statewide debate over growth, affordable housing and home rule. The proposed redevelopment would dramatically transform the Causeway Cove property along Seaway Drive. According to city records, plans call for five towers ranging from 11 to 17 stories, 913 residential units, two hotels totaling 407 rooms, more than 72,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, and 218 marina slips. For residents like Edie Harrison, the project would the area known for its waterfront views, boating access and small-town character. "Everything is still very quaint," Harrison said. "It's one of those gems." Harrison and hundreds of other residents have raised concerns about the size of the development, traffic impacts and what they view as a lack of public input. At the center of the fight is Florida's Live Local Act, a law passed in 2023 to encourage the construction of affordable and workforce housing across the state. The law allows qualifying projects to bypass certain local zoning, density and height restrictions if affordability requirements are met. City officials have repeatedly said the proposed Causeway Cove project qualifies under the law and therefore moves through an administrative review process rather than a traditional public hearing and commission vote. For critics, that process has become one of the most controversial aspects of the proposal. Fort Pierce Commissioner Michael Broderick said residents' concerns extend beyond the size of the development. "The concern is density, traffic flow," Broderick said, pointing to longstanding concerns about capacity on Seaway Drive. Another major debate centers on affordability. Under Live Local, affordable housing calculations are based on regional income levels rather than income levels specific to Fort Pierce. Critics argue the formula can produce rents that technically qualify as affordable under state guidelines but remain difficult for many local residents to afford. According to city officials, some qualifying units could rent for more than $2,300 per month, while Fort Pierce's median rent is substantially lower. Broderick said many residents question whether those figures reflect true affordability within the city. Even some lawmakers who supported the legislation have raised concerns about how it is being applied. Dana Trabulsy, whose district includes parts of the Treasure Coast, has recently questioned whether developments of this scale reflect what legislators intended when they approved the measure. The Fort Pierce dispute is also part of a much larger battle unfolding across Florida. Several lawsuits challenging aspects of the Live Local Act are moving through the courts as cities seek to regain greater authority over local development decisions. Supporters of the law argue it is helping address Florida's housing shortage, while critics contend it has weakened local home-rule powers and limited communities' ability to shape growth. Land-use attorney Keith Poliakoff, who has represented clients in Live Local disputes across the state, said local governments generally have limited discretion once a project satisfies state requirements. Poliakoff said the law effectively requires municipalities to administratively approve qualifying projects, even when residents or local leaders oppose the density, height or scale of a development. State data show more than 200 Live Local projects have been proposed or approved across Florida , making the law one of the most significant growth and housing measures enacted in recent years. Related 2024 article: $100M Kanner Hwy development in Stuart: Affordable housing powered by Live Local Act If things move forward as anticipated, construction on the Causeway Cove development could begin before the end of the year. The property's owner, Palm Beach developer Ashton DePeyster, did not respond to requests for comment. This report is part of an ongoing CBS12 News I-Team investigation examining the impact of Florida's Live Local Act, the legal challenges surrounding the law, and how communities across the Treasure Coast are responding to large-scale development projects.

entry.title: Palm Beach County woman charged with animal cruelty after 11 dogs found in filthy cages at her home
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after investigators said 11 dogs were found living in cages containing accumulated urine and feces inside her home. Leslie Ann Torres, 34, faces seven felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and four misdemeanor counts related to animal abandonment, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office probable cause affidavit. The investigation began Aug. 22 when deputies went to Torres' home located on West Mayaguana Lane in Lake Worth while investigating an unrelated felony matter. Deputies reported smelling a strong odor of urine and feces and hearing numerous dogs barking inside. Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control was called to the home. Investigators said Torres identified 13 dogs as hers, 11 of which she ultimately surrendered to animal control. According to investigators, several dogs were being kept in wire cages containing accumulated feces, urine-soaked clothing and other debris. One cage containing approximately 4 dogs had a strong odor of urine and feces, while another cage was described as having blankets and clothing saturated with urine and feces. Investigators said some of the dogs showed signs of hair loss, skin problems and other medical issues. A veterinarian later examined all 11 surrendered dogs and reported conditions including urine staining and scalding, hair loss, skin infections, flea infestations, anemia, dehydration and malnutrition. Several dogs had body-condition scores of 2 or 3 out of 9, according to the affidavit. entry.summary: Indian River County sheriff announces 50+ arrests in multi-agency human trafficking operation    WPTV
entry.article_text: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operationOperation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday.Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement."Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said.The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said.During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online."Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman accused of elder exploitation, including draining $100K from accounts - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman accused of elder exploitation, including draining $100K from accounts    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 60-year-old woman was arrested after an investigation by the Port St. Lucie Police Department in alleged exploitation and neglect of an elderly and medically vulnerable man. Barbara Baumgarten is accused of draining around $100,000 from the 85-year-old man's bank accounts and listed herself as a co-borrower on a $616,550 mortgage. She is facing felony charges of grand theft from a person 65 years of age or older, exploitation of an elderly person or disabled adult and neglect of an elderly person or disabled adult. Baumgarten was arrested with help from the U.S. On Thursday, she was booked at the St. Lucie County Jail and remains there on $310,000 bond. Her first appearance was Friday. This investigation began on March 18, when an elderly man was found injured on the floor of his Port St. Lucie home by Baumgarten, his caregiver. The victim initially reported that four men had entered his home and assaulted him. Surveillance footage showed no one entering or leaving the property, and no signs of forced entry or theft. He provided inconsistent accounts of what occurred. Detectives determined the victim was experiencing significant cognitive issues. But detectives continued looking into the victim’s overall well-being and circumstances. The investigation shifted toward concerns of elder exploitation and neglect, and grew into the months-long investigation documented in a 45-page investigative report. As the victim’s physical and cognitive health declined, he became increasingly dependent on Baumgarten, investigators found. They determined that Baumgarten had assumed significant control over the victim’s finances and legal affairs, including power of attorney and healthcare surrogate. Detectives also learned the victim had been isolated from family and friends, and that changes had been made to his estate documents that benefited Baumgarten. Records reviewed by detectives showed there was a decline in his financial accounts from $105,971 in March 2023 to approximately $4,897 by April 2026 . Investigators also uncovered a $616,550 mortgage on Baumgarten’s residence in which the victim was listed as a co-borrower. That is despite the property being solely in Baumgarten’s name and evidence that the victim was reportedly unaware his signature appeared on the mortgage. Detectives worked with healthcare providers, caregivers, family members, financial institutions and other agencies to establish the full extent of the circumstances surrounding the victim’s care and finances. The Florida Department of Children and Families ultimately substantiated allegations of exploitation and determined that the victim lacked the capacity to independently make his own decisions. The victim was removed from Baumgarten’s care, placed under a temporary guardianship, and reunited with his family. "This case serves as a reminder of the importance of looking beyond the initial circumstances when something does not appear right," the police agency said in a news release. "Through an extensive investigation, detectives were able to uncover concerns involving the care, finances, and well-being of a vulnerable member of our community and ultimately help ensure his safety. entry.title: Fort Pierce man arrested after raid of illicit drugs worth millions - WPBF
entry.summary: Fort Pierce man arrested after raid of illicit drugs worth millions    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce man was arrested after a raid Friday by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and U.S. Marshals Service found a massive amount of illicit drugs, including fentanyl and cocaine, worth several million dollars. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Special Investigations Division, with assistance from the SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service, executed a narcotics-related search warrant at a residence in the 3100 block of S. 24th Street in Fort Pierce. The subject of the investigation, Tony Saunders, 48, was taken into custody. Saunders, a three-time convicted felon who is on federal probation, also had two active warrants related to the sale and delivery of controlled substances. Afterward, Saunders faced additional charges of trafficking in fentanyl, trafficking in cocaine, trafficking in MDPV, manufacturing cocaine, tampering with evidence and possession of marijuana with intent to sell. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0j4igLYhtX4QpfPCZhHkYeREcfiqd9eehsAoAcjVwDWTipnXHZNWyrJLe6gbwukcvl The search resulted in the seizure of approximately 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl, 303 grams of cocaine, 97 grams of marijuana laced with MDPV, and 60 oxycodone pills totaling approximately 6.2 grams, the sheriff's office said. The street value of 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl can range from $150,000 to nearly $1.8 million, depending heavily on its purity, geographic location, and whether it is sold as wholesale powder or broken down into counterfeit pills, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. The estimated street value of 303 grams of cocaine in the U.S. ranges between roughly $18,180 and $60,600. Detectives also seized assorted ammunition, drug paraphernalia and materials consistent with the preparation and distribution of narcotics. A single kilogram of fentanyl has the potential to kill 500,000 people, making 4.5 kilograms a lethal volume capable of millions of fatal doses, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. “4.5 kilos of fentanyl are 4.5 kilos that will not reach our streets," Sheriff Richard Del Tro said. "Fentanyl is a deadly poison, and those who traffic in it are putting lives at risk for profit. I commend our detectives, SWAT Team, and the U.S. Marshals Service for their commitment to this mission. We will continue to pursue those who traffic dangerous narcotics and do everything within our authority to make St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: Two men arrested after road rage incident leads to shooting in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: Two men arrested after road rage incident leads to shooting in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: Two men were arrested after a road rage incident escalated into a shooting near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace on Sept. 17, 2026, at approximately 6:30 p.m., according to the Port St. Investigators determined the incident began as a misunderstanding between two drivers. One driver believed he was being followed after changing lanes and merging from SW Crosstown Parkway, where the vehicles had crossed paths, and one driver thought the other had cut him off. However, police said the investigation revealed there was no intentional following. One of the drivers, identified as 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as 41-year-old Dean Plotts, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy who was in the area traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was transported to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Detectives responded to the scene and collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, dash cam footage, and other physical evidence. Based on the evidence collected, witness information, video footage, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody in connection with the investigation, which remains ongoing. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law. entry.title: Port St. Lucie woman accused of elder exploitation, including draining $100K from accounts - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie woman accused of elder exploitation, including draining $100K from accounts    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 60-year-old woman was arrested after an investigation by the Port St. Lucie Police Department in alleged exploitation and neglect of an elderly and medically vulnerable man. Barbara Baumgarten is accused of draining around $100,000 from the 85-year-old man's bank accounts and listed herself as a co-borrower on a $616,550 mortgage. She is facing felony charges of grand theft from a person 65 years of age or older, exploitation of an elderly person or disabled adult and neglect of an elderly person or disabled adult. Baumgarten was arrested with help from the U.S. On Thursday, she was booked at the St. Lucie County Jail and remains there on $310,000 bond. Her first appearance was Friday. This investigation began on March 18, when an elderly man was found injured on the floor of his Port St. Lucie home by Baumgarten, his caregiver. The victim initially reported that four men had entered his home and assaulted him. Surveillance footage showed no one entering or leaving the property, and no signs of forced entry or theft. He provided inconsistent accounts of what occurred. Detectives determined the victim was experiencing significant cognitive issues. But detectives continued looking into the victim’s overall well-being and circumstances. The investigation shifted toward concerns of elder exploitation and neglect, and grew into the months-long investigation documented in a 45-page investigative report. As the victim’s physical and cognitive health declined, he became increasingly dependent on Baumgarten, investigators found. They determined that Baumgarten had assumed significant control over the victim’s finances and legal affairs, including power of attorney and healthcare surrogate. Detectives also learned the victim had been isolated from family and friends, and that changes had been made to his estate documents that benefited Baumgarten. Records reviewed by detectives showed there was a decline in his financial accounts from $105,971 in March 2023 to approximately $4,897 by April 2026 . Investigators also uncovered a $616,550 mortgage on Baumgarten’s residence in which the victim was listed as a co-borrower. That is despite the property being solely in Baumgarten’s name and evidence that the victim was reportedly unaware his signature appeared on the mortgage. Detectives worked with healthcare providers, caregivers, family members, financial institutions and other agencies to establish the full extent of the circumstances surrounding the victim’s care and finances. The Florida Department of Children and Families ultimately substantiated allegations of exploitation and determined that the victim lacked the capacity to independently make his own decisions. The victim was removed from Baumgarten’s care, placed under a temporary guardianship, and reunited with his family. "This case serves as a reminder of the importance of looking beyond the initial circumstances when something does not appear right," the police agency said in a news release. "Through an extensive investigation, detectives were able to uncover concerns involving the care, finances, and well-being of a vulnerable member of our community and ultimately help ensure his safety. entry.title: Parts of Palm Beach County still in drought after over 15 inches of rain last week
entry.summary: Parts of Palm Beach County remain in a drought, even after some areas received more than 15 inches of rain in the past week. A new drought update is expected Thursday morning, and there is a good chance some areas in the Palm Beaches will be removed from drought status at that time. Coastal communities on the Treasure Coast have already exited the drought, while parts of the Palm Beaches remain technically in drought a distinction that becomes clear when looking at yearly rainfall totals to date. A couple of months ago, all local counties were in extreme drought. Since then, significant strides have been made, though more rain is still needed to bring the entire region out of drought conditions. Several factors are used to monitor drought, including precipitation and temperature, water supply such as streamflow and reservoir levels and soil moisture.

entry.title: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical
entry.summary: A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon. Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. Sept. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting. The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911. Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket, police said. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm. Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital. No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

WalletHub's new 'Credit Card Debt Study' found consumers added roughly $29 billion in credit card debt during the second quarter of this year. entry.title: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office seeks 2 people after man hospitalized with broken jaw at Luke Bryan concert
entry.summary: The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office is asking for the public's help identifying two individuals in connection with a man being hospitalized after an altercation at a Luke Bryan concert at iTHINK Financial Amphitheater. The incident happened at the concert on Saturday, Sept. 12. WATCH BELOW: Man hospitalized after concert altercation; 2 sought 2 sought after man hospitalized after altercation at Luke Bryan concert The man's daughter said he was punched during the event. She posted a video to TikTok asking for information, which has since been seen by over 150,000 people. 'He's in surgery right now. His jaw is broken in two different places,' she said in the video. She said she hopes someone who was at the concert that night will come forward. 'It would just be really helpful if someone could come forward with some information,' she said. The daughter also shared photos of her father, telling us he had his jaw wired shut following the incident. Earlier this week, she posted an update saying her father has been released from the hospital. 'He does have a long recovery ahead of him,' she said. She is still asking anyone with information to reach out. 'If anybody has any pictures of them in the background, or around or anything please send it over,' she said. The daughter told us the family is unable to do an interview at this time. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office has released photos of the two individuals they are seeking in connection with the incident. entry.title: Tropical Storm Fay weakens in the far eastern Atlantic, expected to be 'fish storm'
entry.summary: Tropical Storm Fay formed in the Atlantic Ocean Sunday morning as the system strengthened hundreds of miles southwest of the Azores. The storm has started to turn more southerly as high pressure builds to its north. TRACKING THE TROPICS:  Hurricane Center  |  Hurricane Guide Increasing wind shear and dry air are causing the storm to weaken. The National Hurricane Center forecasts Fay to become a post-tropical remnant low by Tuesday and dissipate by the end of the week. Fay will be considered a 'fish storm,' as there are no coastal watches or warnings in effect, and the storm currently poses no hazards to land. No other tropical development is expected this week. entry.title: 'You are not alone': Port St. Lucie woman turns grief into community for others
entry.summary: Losing someone you love can change everything. For Stacey Comer, that loss came in 2018 when her husband, Chris, died following complications from a kidney transplant. WATCH You Are Not Alone: PSL woman turns grief into community for others You Are Not Alone: PSL woman turns grief into community for others As she learned to navigate life without him, Comer also began to notice there wasn't one central place on the Treasure Coast where people experiencing grief could go to find support, resources and connection. She started asking herself a simple question: Why isn't there an entity where all of this lives under? That question became the foundation for Chriss Place , a free, in-person grief support community Comer is now creating on the Treasure Coast. Comer said grief can be difficult to understand until you experience it yourself. She added that while friends and family often want to help, people who are grieving can still feel isolated. You only sort of know it if you're in the club, and when you're in the club everyone wants to be so supportive and helpful, Comer said. Chriss Place is intended to give people a place to connect with others who understand what they're going through. The community is not limited to people who have lost a spouse or immediate family member. Comer wants it to be available to anyone who has experienced a loss and needs support navigating what comes next. Right now, Comer is creating Chriss Place from the ground up. Her long-term vision is to create a physical space on the Treasure Coast somewhere that feels comfortable and welcoming, where people can gather, find resources and connect with others who understand grief. You are not alone. You feel alone because you think you're the only one feeling it, but you're not, Comer said. For Comer, Chriss Place is rooted in the loss of her husband but she hopes it can become something much bigger. She wants other people on the Treasure Coast to have the kind of support she realized was missing during her own journey through grief. The ultimate goal is to create a community where people don't have to navigate that journey by themselves. While grief may look different for everyone, Comer wants people to know one thing: They don't have to face it alone. For more information on the next free community grief meet-up, visit their website .

entry.title: Florida governor signs death warrant for William Reaves Jr., convicted of killing Indian River County deputy
entry.summary: Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20, at 6 p.m. WATCH BELOW: Man who killed Indian River Co. deputy to be executed in October Execution date set for man who killed Indian River Co. deputy The Crime Reaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store. Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves's shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face. As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, 'I wouldn't do that if I were you.' The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times. Conviction and Sentencing Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994. Decades of Appeals Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades. In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. However, on Sept. 28, 2017, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied. Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that 'the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant,' and confirmed that 'there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause.' The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20, at 6 p.m.WATCH BELOW: Man who killed Indian River Co. deputy to be executed in OctoberReaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store.Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves's shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face.As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, "I wouldn't do that if I were you." The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times.Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach.The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994.Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades.In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied.Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that "the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant," and confirmed that "there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause."The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

entry.title: Palm Beach Royals trainer teaches pickleball to veterans and first responders in community event
entry.summary: What makes pickleball so special is that everyone can play it, and on Wednesday night, some of America's heroes were learning the game. A dozen former military and first responders spent the day in West Palm Beach learning the fastest-growing sport of pickleball courtesy of the Palm Beach Royals. WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach Royals trainer teaches pickleball to veterans Palm Beach Royals trainer teaches pickleball to veterans As part of our hooking veterans fishing program, weve been coming down to Palm Beach and West Palm, and we decided to bring one of our sporting adventures here with all the great connections we have, said Steve Luppino, the founder of Hyperformance Foundation. Its a national non-profit that connects former military members and first responders to different sporting events. What were trying to do here is build a community, and so introducing them to sports they might find a passion in and can take home and share with their friends, their kiddos, their spouse thats what this is all about, said Luppino. The crew featured about 10-15 vets and first responders, and they all had one thing in common: theyve never played pickleball before. Ive always wanted to give it a go. Im glad that we could bring a group of veterans and just cut loose and have a good time, said Tyler Jeffries, a retired U.S. Army Specialist who lost both of his legs on a mission in southern Afghanistan, when a bomb ambushed him and his platoon. While he uses a wheelchair, hes not letting his disability limit his fun; in fact, he cherishes small wins like playing pickleball, and he's pretty good. Its really not as difficult as it looks on TV or looks anywhere else I see people playing. Im pretty happy I can stay in my chair and have a good time, said Jeffries. They had a good time, but one thing the fellas didnt know was that the Palm Beach Royals Director of Community Events, Nikki Roth, was training them. Were very excited to bring veterans together. Its just so important to see people when they leave the pickleball court feel really good about themselves, and they always ask when's the next event, said Roth. While the guys arent sure when the next event will be, Jeffries knew one thing. I find out that the trainer is actually with the professional team, and right away Im like, Im going to make sure shes on my team, said Jeffries, who showcased good form; he and Roth dominated.

entry.title: Florida fishing charter accidentally reels in missing US military drone near Eglin Air Force Base
entry.summary: Speckled trout, redfish, flounder, mackerel, sharks. These are what you might expect to reel in while fishing off the Florida Panhandle on any given day. But on Saturday, a group aboard a fishing charter was met with an unexpected encounter: a US military drone believed to be a clone of the notorious Iranian-designed Shahed-136. Hot Spots Charters, a fishing charter company out of Pensacola, said on Facebook it made the surprising catch, alongside a photo of the drone against its other, more assuming, snags. 'Great 6 hour today with this crew! If anyone is looking for their drone please call Hot Spots!' charter captain Daniel Arsenault wrote. Another photo showed the drone taking up the entire bow section of the fishing boat. The discovery was reportedly made near Eglin Air Force Base, home of the US Air Force's 96th Test Wing. The Air Force acknowledged a drone was missing from the Eglin inventory, though it would not specify the type, according to defense news site, The War Zone , citing an Eglin AFB spokesperson. 'I can confirm that we were doing a test and the test article went down,' the spokesperson told TWZ. CNN has asked Eglin AFB for comment. Arsenault, seeming unfazed by the catch, told CNN he came across the drone by chance. 'Riding along offshore and saw it floating,' he told CNN. The drone appeared be an FLM 136, a clone of the Iranian-designed Shahed 136, which has played a key role in the Ukraine and Iran wars. The Air Force announced late last year it had cloned the Iranian-designed model, calling them the Low-cost Unmanned Combat Attack System, or LUCAS, drones. Manufactured by Arizona-based Spektreworks, the drones are 9.8 feet (2.9 meters) long, have a wingspan of 8.2 feet, and weigh 70 pounds. US Central Command announced in early March that LUCAS drones were being used in the war with Iran , 'delivering American-made retribution.' The photos shared by Hot Spots Charters showed the drone missing its nose section and propeller in the rear. The company later said on Facebook, 'The black suvs came and got their drone, all is good!' Some anglers appeared to revel in the catch of the day. 'Fun fight but they're super bony and taste like avgas,' one Facebook user wrote. 'Aren't those strictly catch and release?' wrote another. The-CNN-Wire 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros. entry.title: Molly's House marks 30 years of helping Treasure Coast families during medical treatment
entry.summary: Mollys House in Stuart is celebrating 30 years of providing affordable lodging and support services for patients and families receiving medical treatment on the Treasure Coast. The nonprofit organization, located in Stuart's medical district, was founded to help families stay close to doctors, hospitals and treatment providers during difficult medical situations. Leaders with Molly's House said the mission continues to focus on reducing stress for families facing long-term care and recovery. WATCH BELOW: Mollys House celebrates 30 years in Stuart Mollys House celebrates 30 years of helping families in Stuart Kate Wiegerink, a member of the Mollys House board of directors and Molly Sharkey's sister, said the organization also works to educate new doctors, nurses and community members about the services available to patients and families. 'We want people to know these resources exist,' Wiegerink said during the anniversary celebration. Molly's House provides affordable lodging for guests traveling for treatment and also offers a free cancer support program for residents, according to organization leaders. The nonprofit is celebrating the milestone with an open house Monday at its facility on Osceola Street in Stuart. Community members are invited to tour the house and healing garden while learning more about the organizations history and programs. Brandi Patricio, whose son TJ (Timothy) is receiving treatment, shared how the nonprofit has helped her family manage the financial and emotional challenges tied to ongoing medical care. Patricio said having access to affordable lodging reduces anxiety about housing costs during treatment and allows families to focus on recovery and care. In addition to housing support, Molly's House provides weekly free meals to residents to help ease food expenses and preparation during stressful medical situations. Businesses and individuals can become a 'Chef for a Day' and provide an average of 28 meals. The organizations leaders said demand for support services remains strong as more families seek affordable options near treatment centers across South Florida and the Treasure Coast.
