entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    WPEC
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. entry.article_text: A 37-year-old man who was shot during a confrontation outside a Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie is now facing charges after investigators determined he was the primary aggressor in the encounter, according to police. Lucie Police Department said officers responded around 3:43 p.m. 19, to the restaurant at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard after receiving reports of a shooting. When officers arrived, they found Christopher Harris, 37, suffering from a gunshot wound to his upper torso. He was flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where his injuries were determined to be non-life-threatening, police said. The other person involved, identified by police as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while detectives investigated. Officers also recovered a firearm. According to investigators, the encounter began after Harris and Davis had an interaction in the restaurant's parking lot. Police said surveillance video showed Davis entering the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order and Harris following him inside, despite Harris not appearing to place or pick up an order. Police said Harris then followed Davis back outside, where exterior surveillance video showed Harris pushing Davis and advancing toward him as Davis moved backward. Investigators said Harris was armed with a knife during the confrontation, and witnesses reported seeing him with a knife shortly before the shooting. Davis fired one round, striking Harris in the chest, according to police. Harris went back inside the restaurant, where people began providing aid and called 911. Investigators said one knife was recovered after it had been removed from Harris' waistband while people were helping him. Police said another knife was later found in his front pocket. After reviewing surveillance video, physical evidence and witness statements, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor and established probable cause to charge him with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction, according to the department. Because Harris remained hospitalized, police said an arrest affidavit was submitted to the St. He is expected to be booked into the jail after he is medically released. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. entry.title: No. 6 Miami loses RB Marty Brown, WR Joshua Moore for rest of season because of injuries
entry.summary: No. 6 Miami lost running back Marty Brown and wide receiver Joshua Moore for the rest of the season because of injuries, coach Mario Cristobal said Monday, adding that several other key players also got hurt in last weekend's win over Wake Forest. Star wide receiver Malachi Toney, running back Mark Fletcher Jr. and defensive linemen Ahmad Moten were all dealing with injuries at various points of the Hurricanes' 33-20 road victory . Fletcher left the game in the fourth quarter, Toney appeared to be limited in the second half and Moten briefly left with what appeared to be a shoulder issue before returning. Another hit came to the linebacker corps, with Ezekiel Marcelin Jr. who had been rising on the depth chart expected to miss several weeks with a lower-body issue. Marcelin was part of four tackles and had a quarterback hurry in Friday's win. 'We got banged up,' Cristobal said in his weekly radio appearance on the university's flagship station, WQAM. 'An interesting kind of situation.' Miami (3-0) plays host to Central Michigan on Saturday, before resuming Atlantic Coast Conference play at Clemson on Oct. 3. Brown appeared to suffer a serious knee injury while being tackled at the end of a 32-yard run that set up a second-quarter Miami touchdown. Moore who caught a touchdown pass to open the scoring played into the fourth quarter but will be out with an upper-body injury, Cristobal said. Brown was Miami's second-leading rusher behind Fletcher last season when the Hurricanes went to the College Football Playoff title game and had 97 yards on 13 carries this season. Moore had 107 yards on seven catches and two touchdowns in Miami's first three games. Cristobal also indicated that he expected Toney, Fletcher and Moten will be fine, though he said he was awaiting more medical reports from the team's staff in the coming days. 'Some guys got banged up and are in and out,' Cristobal said. 'Certainly not what we wanted.'

entry.summary: 'I'm not going back to prison': New details emerge in Palm City SWAT standoff    WPEC
entry.article_text: Before an hours-long SWAT standoff in Palm City , a man allegedly threatened to kill himself and his ex-girlfriend after she went to his home to check on him following their breakup, a new report reveals. According to an arrest report from the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the ex-girlfriend of the suspect, Darrel Abbey, arrived at his home at about 12:08 p.m. after the two had broken up the previous night. She told investigators Abbey was not doing well mentally and had previously made comments about killing himself. When she arrived, Abbey had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts, according to the report. The woman told investigators Abbey appeared to be extremely intoxicated. The arrest report says Abbey brought both firearms inside the home and began screaming at the woman, "I should die, you should kill me," while holding a gun. Investigators said Abbey continued yelling at the woman while recording the interaction on his phone. The woman told investigators that Abbey pointed the gun at her several times and threatened to kill her and her stepfather. At one point, Abbey allegedly placed the gun under his chin and pulled the trigger, but the firearm did not discharge because the magazine had been removed, according to the report. Investigators said Abbey later began packing his vehicle. Fearing he was going to shoot her stepfather, the woman took the gun away from him, but Abbey allegedly continued reaching for it as she begged him to stop. The report says that when Abbey picked up the gun again, he said, "This is really f***** dangerous now." Investigators said Abbey continued drinking bourbon and Jameson throughout the encounter. As Abbey walked outside, the woman told investigators she heard several loud "pop" sounds. Abbey then returned inside to retrieve a rifle and allegedly tried to get the woman to come outside and shoot it with him. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? When she asked what he was shooting at, Abbey allegedly told her he had hung a bucket from a nearby tree and was shooting at it. At some point during the incident, Abbey allegedly began cleaning the firearms and said, "I gotta wipe all my fingerprints off, I gotta get the gunshot residue off of my hands, I'm not going back to prison." The report says Abbey later attempted to get into his vehicle while continuing to drink, prompting the woman to begin recording him. Investigators who reviewed the video said Abbey appeared intoxicated while sitting in the driver's seat, slurred his words and struggled to hold his head upright. When Abbey realized the woman was recording, he allegedly reached for her phone. The woman then ran down the road until a passing motorist stopped to help her. Deputies later attempted to contact Abbey at the residence, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, leading to an hours-long standoff involving the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and hostage negotiators. Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. Investigators also said Abbey is a convicted felon from Washington state with a prior conviction for vehicular assault.

entry.article_text: A man barricaded with a weapon inside a residence in Palm City was taken into custody after he chased his girlfriend down the road with a gun Saturday afternoon, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office said. Darrel Abbey, 38, was apprehended after leaving the home on Southwest Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road, the sheriff's office posted on Facebook. "The Martin County Sheriff’s Office SWAT Team has safely resolved the armed barricaded subject situation on Southwest Bessey Creek Trail," the agency said. He was taken to the Martin County Jail and booked at 6:57 p.m. He is facing three charges: felony aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill (domestic), misdemeanor battery (domestic) and misdemeanor use of a firearm under the influence of alcohol. https://www.facebook.com/MartinCountySheriffsOffice/posts/pfbid0UhZCMdUMpppSpxntWNQ2nc5uVBuTDK6zfE7YKBDU9gjfPz4XcNqwzeLRwj8kP6jbl Shortly after 3 p.m., the sheriff's office took a call from a frantic woman who said she was chased down the street by a man, who went into the backyard and fired multiple shots, Sheriff John Budensiek told WPBF's Caleb Califano at the scene. He said he threatened to kill her. Multiple people around the neighborhood then called 911. Callers indicated the incident was domestic-related and involved an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon inside the residence, the sheriff's office said. The man was described as "armed and dangerous" inside the home. Sheriff's office road patrol, detectives, SWAT and the hostage negotiation team were on the scene working to safely resolve the situation, the agency said. "He wouldn't talk to them," Budensiek said. "So eventually our SWAT team was called to this location to try to resolve this scenario peacefully. "But this is where all the tools and the resources that we have come into play to keep the county residents safe." The SWAT team used a loudspeaker to order him out. When he refused, the sheriff's office pumped gas into the house. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

McCaffrey's two 1-yard TDs in a 35-13 win over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday made him the fourth-fastest player in the Super Bowl era to reach 100 career touchdowns and the third player ever with at least 50 TDs with two franchises. It means a lot, McCaffrey said. It's a blessing to be able to play this game and stuff like that is always cool. But it's always about the team and showing up and doing your job. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell agrees on a 4-year contract extension McCaffrey didn't have to do a lot on Sunday, a day when Brock Purdy and the rest of the offense was clicking at such a high level that the Niners scored touchdowns on their first five drives. McCaffrey started it with a 1-yard run in the first quarter and capped the scoring for San Francisco late in the third when he scored again from 1-yard out. He finished with 23 yards on 10 carries and four catches for 43 yards. CMC, hes just the GOAT, linebacker Fred Warner said. GOATs do things like that. Its just another day at the office for old Christian. But nobody works harder on their craft and is as dedicated to the game as Christian. Everything that he does, hes earned it and hes only going to continue to keep getting better. Marshall Faulk was somebody that I’ve probably seen every single snap he’s played. I don’t take it for granted. Randy Moss I played with a ton of times with Madden growing up. Those are huge, huge honors.”MORE NFL NEWS | NFL ends the Pro Bowl game, but players will still be honored as Pro BowlersMcCaffrey's career is full of noteworthy accomplishments already. I grew up watching him in high school and stuff when he was at Stanford and then the Panthers and then to be a teammate with him and be there when he scored his 100th touchdown was insane,” Purdy said. "It’s really cool to think about that. To be on his team and be a teammate with him and go and help him do what he wants to do with his career and just be there and feed him the ball and stuff, it’s an honor for me."

entry.article_text: A confrontation in a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical parking lot ended with a man shot in the upper torso and later facing charges. 19, officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded to the Pollo Tropical at 1635 NW St. Lucie West Blvd., where they found Christopher Harris suffering from gunshot wounds to his upper torso, according to a news release. The shooting led to a heavy law enforcement investigation outside the business , with crime scene tape around the restaurant. The other person involved, identified as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while officers investigated. Police also recovered and secured a firearm. PSLPD said interviews and surveillance video from the restaurant showed the confrontation between Harris and Davis began after the two men had an interaction in the parking lot. Davis entered the restaurant to pick up a delivery order, and Harris followed him inside despite not appearing to place or pick up an order, police said. When Davis left the restaurant, Harris allegedly followed him outside. Police said surveillance video showed Harris, who was armed with a knife, push Davis and then advance toward him as Davis backed away. Davis then pulled out a gun and fired one round, striking Harris in the upper torso, according to PSLPD. Harris returned to the restaurant, where people began rendering aid and called 911. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? During the investigation, officers recovered one knife from Harris' waistband while aid was being provided and another from his front pocket, police said. Harris was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Based on surveillance video, witness statements and other evidence, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor, according to PSLPD. He was charged with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction. Police said Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail once he is medically released from the hospital.

entry.article_text: Florida's Treasure Coast earned its name from Spanish coins that washed ashore centuries ago — and the legendary treasure hunters who came to collect them.Melvin Fisher-Abt is the grandson and namesake of one of America's most celebrated treasure hunters, Mel Fisher."I was born in 1997 and Mel passed in 1998 and out of all of the grandkids I was given the namesake Mel and I feel really connected to my grandfather in that way — definitely have big shoes to fill," Fisher-Abt said.His grandfather was a man whose dedication and determination rewrote the history books. His discoveries were so remarkable that Johnny Carson invited him to share his story with millions of viewers on "The Tonight Show.'Mel Fisher walked on stage wearing one of his favorite finds — a gold wedding chain."That's how he would look when he was sitting at the bar — draped in gold chains with gold bars," Fisher-Abt said.But before the fame and fortune came persistence, perseverance, and personal loss.Mel Fisher made his first discovery off the coast of Vero Beach, where over 1,000 gold coins were unearthed from the sunken 1715 Spanish Treasure Fleet."Gold is a noble metal and will be just as shiny as the day it went down — gold shines forever is what my grandfather used to say," Fisher-Abt said.In the 1600s and 1700s, Spanish fleets sailed annually from Spain to the Caribbean with a threefold mission."They were trying to extract wealth from the new world and bring it back to Spain to fund European wars and debts — they were trying to promote Catholicism," Fisher-Abt said. "They were trying to conquer land for the kingdom of Spain — so 'God, Glory and Gold' was their mission."When some of those fleets shipwrecked in major storms, Florida became a hotspot for treasure hunters. One of them — the Spanish galleon Nuestra Señora de Atocha — sank in a powerful hurricane in 1622 off the coast of Key West.Mel Fisher moved his family and crew to the Florida Keys specifically to search for the Atocha's buried treasure."Initially, he believed they would find it in six months and after six months he said alright maybe a year — and after a year he said alright maybe we'll be here for awhile," Fisher-Abt said. "He was an eternal optimist."In 1973, Mel Fisher found a 14-foot galleon anchor he believed was from the Atocha."Everyday he would wake up and say today is the day — cause he believed it in his bones that one musket ball and one silver coin and an anchor would lead to a huge pile of treasure," Fisher-Abt said.It was another 12 years before Mel and his team found the massive Atocha "Mother Lode" — an estimated $400 million to $450 million in gold, silver, coins, and emeralds.But before the big find came the greatest test of Mel's determination, when tragedy struck. In 1975, their salvage vessel capsized and three crew members perished, including his eldest son."If there was ever a stopping point that my grandfather really considered giving up the hunt losing my uncle Dirk was that point in time," Fisher-Abt said.Yet Mel chose to honor his son's memory by continuing the quest they shared."When he did get back to the site it was a renewed sense of finishing the job," Fisher-Abt said.He found the Atocha's main treasure pile exactly 10 years to the day after his greatest loss. The search continues to this day."Along the way we've recovered all kinds of artifacts — religious artifacts — some of them are very intricate some are preserved very well deep in the mud," Fisher-Abt said.According to Fisher-Abt, there is still much more to be found."The research that's been done and the work that's been done by the people before us is true and faithful and that everything they've done will pan out for us — there is another 20 tons of silver at the end of the rainbow," Fisher-Abt said.For more information about Mel Fisher's Treasures, click here.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    WPEC
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. entry.article_text: A confrontation in a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical parking lot ended with a man shot in the upper torso and later facing charges. 19, officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded to the Pollo Tropical at 1635 NW St. Lucie West Blvd., where they found Christopher Harris suffering from gunshot wounds to his upper torso, according to a news release. The shooting led to a heavy law enforcement investigation outside the business , with crime scene tape around the restaurant. The other person involved, identified as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while officers investigated. Police also recovered and secured a firearm. PSLPD said interviews and surveillance video from the restaurant showed the confrontation between Harris and Davis began after the two men had an interaction in the parking lot. Davis entered the restaurant to pick up a delivery order, and Harris followed him inside despite not appearing to place or pick up an order, police said. When Davis left the restaurant, Harris allegedly followed him outside. Police said surveillance video showed Harris, who was armed with a knife, push Davis and then advance toward him as Davis backed away. Davis then pulled out a gun and fired one round, striking Harris in the upper torso, according to PSLPD. Harris returned to the restaurant, where people began rendering aid and called 911. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? During the investigation, officers recovered one knife from Harris' waistband while aid was being provided and another from his front pocket, police said. Harris was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Based on surveillance video, witness statements and other evidence, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor, according to PSLPD. He was charged with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction. Police said Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail once he is medically released from the hospital.

entry.title: Boca Raton golfer Frankie Harris aims for PGA Tour after record-setting college career
entry.summary: Boca Raton native Frankie Harris is making a name for himself in professional golf, winning a Korn Ferry Tour title just months into his pro career and setting his sights on the PGA Tour. Harris grew up with golf in his blood. His father was a professional golfer, and Harris had a club in his hands almost from birth. WATCH BELOW: Boca Raton golfer sets sights on PGA Tour Boca Raton golfer sets sights on PGA Tour 'I had a golf club in my hands at a very young age. My father was a professional golfer,' Harris said. He began his golf journey around age 8, quickly making a name for himself as a junior golfer. 'I stacked up a lot of wins as a junior golfer. I've kind of always known deep down that I had something pretty special,' Harris said. Harris went on to win several national and local tournaments before entering high school at Boca Raton, where he discovered a new dimension of the game. 'Golf is an individual sport, so having teammates and playing for something bigger than yourself was something pretty interesting to me,' Harris said. His dominance continued at the high school level, where he won regionals, qualified for state and earned player of the year honors. After one year at Auburn, Harris transferred to the University of South Carolina, where he built a dynasty, setting school records over his college career. 'To stack up six wins throughout my career, there was definitely a special thing,' Harris said. After graduating, Harris turned pro and wasted no time making an impact. He won a Korn Ferry Tour title just months into his professional career, shooting a historic round in the process. 'Kind of reached my flow state. I never shot a 59 before, and I was fortunate to do that on Sunday,' Harris said. His 12-under 59 secured the title and put him on a fast track toward the PGA Tour. Harris said returning to Broken Sound in southern Palm Beach County, where his golf journey began, carries special meaning. 'It's always great being back in South Florida; it's my favorite place in the world; it's somewhere where I want to stay the rest of my life,' Harris said.

entry.title: Former NYPD officer who worked Ground Zero now leads Martin County school safety - wptv.com
entry.summary: Former NYPD officer who worked Ground Zero now leads Martin County school safety    wptv.com
entry.article_text: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. "There are thousands upon thousands of stories. This is just mine," he said. "Everybody says that time heals all, and I know for me and everybody who was down there -- we're still waiting."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operationOperation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday.Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement."Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said.The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said.During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online."Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked."We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said.Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County."We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said.FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county."This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said.Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors."Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today."FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. entry.title: Former Carefree and JetRide boat club employees describe working conditions before closures
entry.summary: Following reporting on the closures of JetRide and Carefree Boat Club locations in Palm Beach County and on the Treasure Coast, two former employees are now speaking out about their experiences working at the clubs. Zachariah Rowland is a former training captain for Carefree Boat Club in Fort Pierce, who also worked as a dockhand at other locations in Florida, but was later terminated. WATCH BELOW: Ex-employees speak out after boat club closures Former boat club employees speak out following closures Rowland reached out to WPTV after our reporting on the closures and the issues members experienced at the docks. Rowland said employees were left to face frustrated members without support from management. 'We're right there with the members, getting essentially yelled at by the members. They're upset, they're frustrated, rightfully so, and we would have to take the brunt of it, not JetRide or Carefree management.' Rowland said. Despite the difficult conditions, Rowland said the members were what he loved about the job. 'The members were the reason why I kept going,' Rowland said. 'It was a hard place to work.' Thomas Margait worked at JetRide in Stuart and at other locations in South Florida. He said employees tried to do right by members, but leadership let them down. 'We did try to provide a good service, and, unfortunately, I feel management failed us,' Margait said. Margait said members deserve accountability. 'They need to have an answer or a resolution,' Margait said. On Sept. 9, JetRide and Carefree Boat Club sent emails to members saying that effective Sept. 1, they ceased operations, citing rising costs and weather disruptions. WPTV has continued to reach out to the owners of JetRide and Carefree Boat Club about these concerns since earlier this month, and we're still working on a response. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.article_text: Crews in the Indian Trail Improvement District are working early mornings and late nights to pump down elevated water levels after days of heavy rain, but officials say garbage clogging drainage canals is making a tough job even harder.Board President Elizabeth Accomando said Monday that while "pumping and dumping," as her crews call it, has been continuous since last week's flooding, water levels in key impoundments remain above where they should be.WATCH BELOW: Trash clogs canals, prompting more flooding concerns"The south impoundment, we're almost a foot above where we like to be, and the north impoundment is still about almost 2 feet above where we'd like it to be," Accomando said. "They're going to continually pump."Lightning and fresh rainfall have slowed progress, but Accomando said an avoidable problem is also hindering the system: trash and yard debris blocking pipes and canals.Standing along one of the district's canals, Accomando pointed to items floating in the water as an example of what crews are pulling out."As you can see, we've got the cooler. It looks like we've got some other personal items, a lot of bottles, just a lot of trash that maybe people are just throwing out their car window as they're going by, or it ends up in the swale and then flows through, and this is where it ends up," she said.On one property, crews found an entire bag of softballs shoved into a pipe. Other times, they've hauled out deflated balls, toys and even coconuts."That clogs up the whole system," Accomando said. "The water backflows into people's properties, so we're up against that as well. Cleaning it out."When crews have to stop to clear blockages, it delays efforts to keep water moving out of flooded neighborhoods.Accomando stressed that while the district manages more than 1,000 miles of canals, swales and ditches, residents have an important role in keeping water flowing."People don't think it's their responsibility," she said. "It's still your land, it's still your residence. So again, if you're able, just be mindful of those things."She urged residents to rake up vegetation left behind after curbside pickup and to keep swales clear so debris doesn't wash into drainage pipes."If you've got a lot of vegetation on the swale for SWA to pick it up, they leave a lot of that debris behind. Try and rake it up if you're able to, because eventually that's going to end up in the pipe and it's going to clog the pipe," she said.The district office, which serves about 17,000 resident-owned lots, is fielding "hundreds and hundreds of calls," she added, and staff are working to return voicemails and emails as quickly as possible."You have to have a little patience right now because we're trying to accommodate so many people at once," she said.Accomando said newer residents, especially those who moved in over the last few relatively dry years, may not realize that the community was intentionally designed to hold water on individual properties."The way that The Acreage was designed, it's designed for you to hold water on your property," she said. "The houses are higher than the lot. You've got low areas that are depressed. The water is going to remain there until the ground can absorb it, which you want because we have to recharge our aquifers. We're all on well water."Swales may move water in some areas and simply hold it in others, she said, but all of it is part of a larger system that has to function together."Water is like gold these days," Accomando said. "You don't want to get rid of any more than you have to."The original design for the area dates back to the 1950s, long before anyone envisioned how large the community — or its surrounding development — would become.Historically, house pads were raised slightly and ponds were dug on lots as a critical drainage feature."You want to have a pond. You shouldn't fill your pond in," Accomando said. "It's all part of the system."As building requirements changed, Palm Beach County began requiring higher house pads and engineered drainage plans to keep water on-site. Problems arise, she said, when residents bring in fill or build structures without following those plans or constructing berms to contain runoff."What we see happening, the higher properties are sending the water to the neighbors who are lower, and they're not building their berm, or they're removing their berm," she said.Accomando described a recent complaint from a resident whose neighbor built a shed that met distance requirements from the property line but sat on an elevated pad with no berm."All that water and all that sand from his base is all washing in and creating a major issue for the next-door neighbor," she said. "We all live here together. We have to work together and be mindful that what we're doing is affecting the person down the line."With large portions of some yards still underwater, mosquitoes are an inevitable concern."When you've got a good portion of your yard [underwater], what are you going to do?" Accomando said.She recommended residents dump standing water in small containers, like garbage can lids and plant saucers, and use commercially available mosquito "dunks" or larvicide products in larger areas of standing water."The wading birds will come in. They'll eat a lot of it," she said, but noted the district cannot eliminate mosquitoes and mosquito-borne disease risks entirely. "We're not going to be able to stop the mosquitoes, and that's way beyond Indian Trails' purview."She also urged residents to protect themselves at dusk with appropriate clothing or insect repellent.As crews continue around-the-clock efforts to bring water levels down, Accomando's message to residents is one of shared responsibility and long-term thinking.She said something as simple as how someone disposes of coconuts from their yard can have a downstream effect — literally."We're seeing a ton of coconuts in the canals. We're seeing them in the pipes. That is not how you dispose of your coconuts," she said.Instead, she suggested residents stack unwanted coconuts in their swale and label them for others to take."If you don't want to eat them, pile them up in your swale. Put a post out there, 'Hey, curb alert! Free coconuts,'" she said. "There are people that want them. Maybe they'll plant them."Above all, she said, residents should remember they are part of a larger drainage network."Please don't just disperse them into the system like this, because again, we all have to work together and be mindful of each other," Accomando said. "The things that you do today might flood your neighbor tomorrow."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Delray Beach mayor says he's against raising property tax rate
entry.summary: Delray Beach Mayor Tom Carney says he's not in favor of raising the city millage rate on the city's homeowners, since taxes may already be going up because of rising property values. 'Even if we do nothing, we just keep the current millage, the residents are going to pay almost 7% more in taxes,' he says. WATCH: Delray Beach mayor says he's against raising property tax rate Delray Beach mayor says no to raising tax rate City commissioners will decide on the tax rate on Tuesday. According to Carney, Delray Beach benefits from rising property values, a busy business district on Atlantic Avenue and new developments in the pipeline. 'We know they're gonna be on the tax rolls in 2027, we know they're gonna be on the tax rolls in 2028.' Under state law, Carney is not taking a position on Amendment 3, the voter referendum that aims to raise the Homestead Exemption and lower property tax bills across Florida. He admits if it passes there will be an impact, and the city has placed signs reminding residents of what property taxes mean for the city. 'I think that there was an overall sense that we need to rein in these expenses and we need to force municipalities to do what others are doing, which is figure out ways to save money,' Carney says.

entry.title: Jolly rules out debates with Donalds, setting off new clash in Florida governor’s race
entry.summary: Democrat David Jolly says he will not debate Republican Byron Donalds before the Nov. 3 election, leaving Florida's two major-party nominees for governor arguing over why they have yet to share a stage. Jolly announced his decision Sunday, accusing Donalds of acting in bad faith and arguing that a debate would deepen political division. Donalds says Jolly is avoiding scrutiny of his property insurance proposal and other policies. WATCH BELOW: Jolly rules out debates with Donalds, setting off new clash Jolly rules out debates with Donalds, setting off new clash 'I think he's acting with bad faith and continues to peddle lies. And Rev, you can't debate a liar,' Jolly told Rev. Al Sharpton on MS NOW over the weekend. The campaigns had accepted different debate invitations, but never agreed to the same events. Jolly accepted proposed forums with CBS Miami's Jim DeFede and the Tampa Tiger Bay Club. Donalds announced he had accepted three other events involving Spectrum News and Florida AM University, News4Jax, and Telemundo and NBC 6. Donalds' campaign said its proposed debates would feature two podiums and no audience. Jolly's campaign said it learned of those arrangements through a news release. 'Byron refused them and instead set his own rules by press release,' Jolly said in a statement about the invitations he had accepted. Donalds responded by pointing to Jolly's earlier willingness to debate him. 'I said 3 debates. Jolly said 12 debates. Yesterday, Jolly said no debates. Who's the liar Dave?' Donalds wrote in a post on X . Jolly's statement also linked to fact-checks of Donalds' campaign attacks. In one, PolitiFact rated false a claim that Jolly wants higher taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security. The dispute comes after Donalds declined calls to debate his Republican primary opponents . At a Florida Chamber event, he compared the campaign to applying for a job. 'If I'm applying for a job, it's not my responsibility to help my competitor get a job interview,' Donalds said. Jolly is now citing that reasoning, saying it is not his job to give Donalds a platform. He said his campaign has held more than 300 town halls and community meetings and will continue meeting voters and conducting online outreach. He said his campaign has held more than 300 town halls and community meetings and will continue meeting voters and conducting online outreach.Political analyst Dr. Susan MacManus said debates offer candidates free exposure and give voters, including those still undecided, a chance to compare the contenders directly."You'll have an unfiltered look at yourself and your opponent side by side," she said.MacManus said declining interest in politics and lengthy televised events can reduce debates' appeal. entry.title: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical
entry.summary: A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon. Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. Sept. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting. The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911. Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket, police said. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm. Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital. No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

WalletHub's new 'Credit Card Debt Study' found consumers added roughly $29 billion in credit card debt during the second quarter of this year. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911. Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket, police said. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm. Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital. No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

entry.title: 'You are not alone': Port St. Lucie woman turns grief into community for others
entry.summary: Losing someone you love can change everything. For Stacey Comer, that loss came in 2018 when her husband, Chris, died following complications from a kidney transplant. WATCH You Are Not Alone: PSL woman turns grief into community for others You Are Not Alone: PSL woman turns grief into community for others As she learned to navigate life without him, Comer also began to notice there wasn't one central place on the Treasure Coast where people experiencing grief could go to find support, resources and connection. She started asking herself a simple question: Why isn't there an entity where all of this lives under? That question became the foundation for Chriss Place , a free, in-person grief support community Comer is now creating on the Treasure Coast. Comer said grief can be difficult to understand until you experience it yourself. She added that while friends and family often want to help, people who are grieving can still feel isolated. You only sort of know it if you're in the club, and when you're in the club everyone wants to be so supportive and helpful, Comer said. Chriss Place is intended to give people a place to connect with others who understand what they're going through. The community is not limited to people who have lost a spouse or immediate family member. Comer wants it to be available to anyone who has experienced a loss and needs support navigating what comes next. Right now, Comer is creating Chriss Place from the ground up. Her long-term vision is to create a physical space on the Treasure Coast somewhere that feels comfortable and welcoming, where people can gather, find resources and connect with others who understand grief. You are not alone. You feel alone because you think you're the only one feeling it, but you're not, Comer said. For Comer, Chriss Place is rooted in the loss of her husband but she hopes it can become something much bigger. She wants other people on the Treasure Coast to have the kind of support she realized was missing during her own journey through grief. The ultimate goal is to create a community where people don't have to navigate that journey by themselves. While grief may look different for everyone, Comer wants people to know one thing: They don't have to face it alone. For more information on the next free community grief meet-up, visit their website .

entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. entry.title: 'Let it go': Port St. Lucie police chief talks about road rage incident that ended with gunfire - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Let it go': Port St. Lucie police chief talks about road rage incident that ended with gunfire    WPBF
entry.article_text: More details are being released about a road rage incident in Port St. Lucie that escalated into a shooting Thursday evening, resulting in one man being injured and both drivers arrested on felony charges. Lucie police received a 911 call around 6:30 p.m. reporting gunshots in a residential neighborhood near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace. "Gunshots in front of my house," a caller said during the emergency call. The caller also described the aftermath of the shooting. "I heard it, and then I saw a guy raising his hands up and said he had blood on his hands," the caller said. Investigators said the altercation began as a misunderstanding during a lane change and merge near SW Crosstown Parkway. The situation escalated into a physical confrontation when 41-year-old Dean Plotts exited his vehicle, approached 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, who was seated in his car, and punched him through the window. "He stepped out of his vehicle, approached the other man who was seated inside his vehicle, and punched him inside his vehicle, so now he's breaking the plane of the window," the Port St. Lucie police chief Leo Niemczyk said. "Therefore, entering, which makes it a burglary of the conveyance with the intention of committing a crime, being battery by punching the other individual who is seated inside the vehicle." Plotts then returned to his vehicle, but the confrontation escalated further. "Almost makes it back to his vehicle and starts getting fire on," Niemczyk said. Police said Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Both men were arrested, with Plotts facing charges for initiating the physical altercation and Kukielka for firing his weapon. When asked if Kukielka’s actions could be considered self-defense, Niemczyk said, "It's not self-defense at that point. If Plotts had been coming at him at that point, the shooting may well have been justified, but it was actually just the reverse. He was fleeing from him." Both men are now facing felony charges. Because one thought the other one may have cut the other one off when they were both turning into the same roadway. Again, no reason to be facing felony charges; let it go, let it go," Niemczyk said. entry.title: Former Fox News producer Jennifer Eckhart dies by suicide in Martin County - WPBF
entry.summary: Former Fox News producer Jennifer Eckhart dies by suicide in Martin County    WPBF
entry.article_text: Jennifer Eckhart, a popular podcaster and former associate producer at Fox Business, died by suicide at her home in Hobe Sound on Saturday morning, according to the Martin County sheriff. Sheriff John Budensiek said he usually doesn't comment on suicides but decided to speak publicly about Eckhart’s death to address conspiracy theories suggesting she had been murdered. "Looking at the scene and going through the investigation, we spent a lot of time. We investigated it as if it was a homicide. Unfortunately, she took her life at her own hands," Budensiek said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Eckhart gained notoriety after accusing a Fox News anchor of raping her. Investigators said she had family and friends who tried to help her, but she had been in and out of mental health facilities and had stopped taking her medications. If you'd like to talk to someone at 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast, you can dial 211. If you'd like to text the helpline, you can message your ZIP code to 898211. Elizabeth Burrows, director of development and communications with 211 Palm Beach and Treasure Coast, emphasized the tragedy of suicide and encouraged those struggling to seek help. "Every death by suicide is a tragedy," Burrows said. She noted that anyone in crisis can call 211 or 988, which are available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, to provide resources or someone to talk to. "You'd be surprised at how often just having someone who's there to listen can help someone make it through their darkest moments," Burrows said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Burrows also stressed the importance of being present and asking questions when supporting someone who may be struggling. Asking about it does not make suicide more of a risk for them. If anything, it lets that person know that they are not alone," she said. "The one answer I can always give is to never give up. As long as someone is still here, there is still an opportunity to support and assist them." The sheriff said Eckhart’s death remains an open investigation as they await toxicology results, but he emphasized that all evidence points to suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available by dialing 211 or 988 for confidential support and resources. If you or someone you know needs help, you can talk with the Suicide Crisis Lifeline by calling or sending a text message to 988, or you can chat online here.

entry.title: Man armed with knives shot outside Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical later charged, police say - cw34.com
entry.summary: Man armed with knives shot outside Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical later charged, police say    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A confrontation in a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical parking lot ended with a man shot in the upper torso and later facing charges. 19, officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded to the Pollo Tropical at 1635 NW St. Lucie West Blvd., where they found Christopher Harris suffering from gunshot wounds to his upper torso, according to a news release. The shooting led to a heavy law enforcement investigation outside the business , with crime scene tape around the restaurant. The other person involved, identified as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while officers investigated. Police also recovered and secured a firearm. PSLPD said interviews and surveillance video from the restaurant showed the confrontation between Harris and Davis began after the two men had an interaction in the parking lot. Davis entered the restaurant to pick up a delivery order, and Harris followed him inside despite not appearing to place or pick up an order, police said. When Davis left the restaurant, Harris allegedly followed him outside. Police said surveillance video showed Harris, who was armed with a knife, push Davis and then advance toward him as Davis backed away. Davis then pulled out a gun and fired one round, striking Harris in the upper torso, according to PSLPD. Harris returned to the restaurant, where people began rendering aid and called 911. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? During the investigation, officers recovered one knife from Harris' waistband while aid was being provided and another from his front pocket, police said. Harris was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Based on surveillance video, witness statements and other evidence, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor, according to PSLPD. He was charged with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction. Police said Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail once he is medically released from the hospital.

entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a massive data center in Indiantown is back before the public with significant changes, but the developers’ new plan has not eased the concerns of many residents who fear the project will harm their community.Representatives for “Project Silver Fox,” a 606-acre data processing center proposed by developers Panatonni and Ferreira, held an open house Monday to present the plan. WATCH: Indiantown 'Project Silver Fox' data center plan returns with changes, resident concerns remainThe debate over the project highlights a familiar tension in growing communities: the promise of economic development versus the desire to maintain a community’s character, with a final decision by the Village Council expected to shape Indiantown's future for years to come.The project was initially withdrawn in April. Now, developers say they have directly addressed the public’s biggest worries.Adam Kramer, an executive with Project Silver Fox, said the new plan includes several key commitments intended to mitigate the facility's impact.“It’s a waterless data center,” Kramer stated, emphasizing that the project would not use Indiantown’s water resources. He also noted changes to the facility’s design and footprint. “We have commitments on how we are doing natural landscaping with retaining the trees there to kind of block the view of the data center, working on the size of the facility.”The project is slated for land already zoned for industrial use, the former site of a power plant. According to project officials, noise levels will remain within village code, there will be no ongoing vibrations, and local water pressure will not be affected.Proponents of the data center point to its potential to transform the local economy without costing taxpayers. Kramer said the project could represent a billion-dollar investment in the village.“What the project is, is an economic opportunity for the community and creating jobs, creating tax revenue,” Kramer said.That view is shared by Kloee Ciuperger, the CEO of the Economic Council of Indiantown.“I think a huge part of the benefits is gonna be that tax revenue,” Ciuperger said. “That’s gonna be able to go to youth, athletics, to parks, to the water infrastructure, to the wastewater infrastructure.”However, some residents at the open house remained skeptical of the developers' motives.“This is a money grab, a land grab and we do not want this,” said Penny Kaminsky-Preli. Despite the proposed changes, many who attended the meeting voiced continuing concerns about the impact of a large-scale data center on their daily lives.Penny Kaminsky-Preli, an Indiantown resident, said the facility is too close to homes and a local school.“First of all they’re way too close to people. There’s a school within 2.2 miles from this place,” Kaminsky-Preli said. “You’re gonna subject teachers to that 5 days a week? The sound, The heat?”Concerns about constant noise, heat generated by the facility, and the overall impact on farmland and families were the primary reasons for the continued opposition.The future of the Project Silver Fox site plan now rests with the Indiantown Village Council, which is expected to make a decision in the coming months, according to Kramer.If approved, construction could begin in phases as early as 2027.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
