The spending puts national party resources behind an incumbent Republicans targeted with the new boundaries.Inside Elections moved Castor’s race to a toss-up on Sept. 17, following an earlier shift from lean Republican to tilt Republican. The forecaster rated the district solid Democratic before the redraw, underscoring how much more competitive her reelection contest has become.The latest changes extend beyond Tampa. 22 Power Rankings, Fox News shifted seven Florida congressional races toward Democrats. Jared Moskowitz’s race in the 25th District moved from toss-up to lean Democratic, while Republican María Elvira Salazar’s race in the 27th moved from likely Republican to lean Republican.Fox attributed the changes largely to national polling favoring Democrats and movement toward the party among Hispanic voters.During the redistricting debate in April, political consultant Michael Worley warned that Republican advantages on paper would not necessarily translate into November victories.“These districts, while they might look Republican on paper, could very well be a key swing vote come November and deliver a Democratic majority back to the House,” Worley said in an April 27 interview.Worley, CEO of MDW Communications, pointed to uncertainty surrounding voters who had backed Republicans in previous elections.“Well, they’re making a big bet that non-Cuban Hispanics are going to continue voting for Republicans. And that is not a given,” he said.Analysts also warned during the April debate that moving Democratic and independent voters into surrounding Republican districts could make some existing GOP seats more competitive.Gov. Ron DeSantis defended the redraw in August, calling it a “good map,” while acknowledging a different political environment from the one Republicans faced in 2022.“This year they’re winnable, but I think it’s going to require some effort,” DeSantis said of the four targeted seats.The ratings changes do not establish that redistricting caused the movement, and seven shifts toward Democrats do not mean seven seats will change parties. Falling short of four Republican pickups would not, by itself, demonstrate that the map cost the GOP seats.In a July 13 interview, political scientist Susan MacManus emphasized that Democrats would have to turn enthusiasm into votes.“Turnout is a huge issue. That’s how you win elections,” MacManus said.For now, “dummymander” remains a political argument. Voters will decide the races Nov.

entry.article_text: Three teens have been arrested in the shooting death of a 17-year-old girl who police say was killed during a planned robbery disguised as a gun sale on West 36th Street last month.Riviera Beach police announced the arrests during a Tuesday morning news conference, calling the case a "senseless and tragic homicide" that has shaken the community. The shooting happened Aug. 21, when officers found the teen with a gunshot wound to the head. She later died of her injuries.WATCH BELOW: 3 teens arrested after 17-year-old fatally shot in Riviera BeachAccording to investigators, the three teens allegedly arranged to meet the victim to buy a firearm she was trying to sell. Police say the suspects instead planned to rob her, and the attempted robbery escalated into deadly violence."This case has shocked this community and shocked me as well," Riviera Beach Police chief Michael Coleman said. "We had several young men go out to commit a dangerous, violent act and subsequently shoot and kill someone in their community."The victim and suspects are all from the same general area and may have known each other in passing, but police said they do not believe they were friends. Detectives said communication leading up to the meeting took place over social media.Police did not release the names of the suspects or the victim, citing their ages and the ongoing investigation. One suspect is 17, and the other two are 16, officials said. All attend schools within the Palm Beach County school system.Because the suspects are minors facing potential capital charges, their names will not be released unless and until they are formally processed through the legal system as adults, police said. The victim's name and address are also being withheld at this stage.Two of the three suspects have prior contact with law enforcement and have "been in the system for a couple years now," according to the chief.WATCH BELOW: Police hold news conference to announce arrestsInvestigators credited a combination of technology and interagency cooperation with helping identify and locate the suspects. That included the use of Flock license plate reader cameras, which spotted a vehicle leaving the crime scene area."As soon as the car left the area, we have a lot of technology in this city, and we were able to track that vehicle to their home," Coleman said.One suspect was arrested in Jacksonville with the help of the U.S. Marshals Service after police learned he had left the area. The other two were taken into custody in Riviera Beach. Officials said marshals were brought in because they can operate across jurisdictions and assist if suspects flee the region.Police declined to say whether the suspects brought their own gun to the meeting or used the weapon that was supposed to be sold, and whether that firearm has been recovered, citing the need to protect the integrity of the investigation. Detectives have interviewed all three defendants, but investigators would not discuss the extent of their cooperation.Officials also said they are still working to determine how the 17-year-old victim obtained the gun she was allegedly selling."We look at all leads," the chief said, adding that in many cases juveniles obtain guns from parents or relatives. "If we find that anybody was involved with this, especially a parent, we're going to pursue criminal charges."The case remains active, and additional arrests or charges are possible, police said.Coleman linked the case to a broader rise in youth violence across Florida, saying Riviera Beach is "no different from any other city" struggling with teens engaging in “adult acts” such as armed robberies.He said social media plays a significant role, not only in coordinating crimes but also in fueling trends such as large "teen takeover" gatherings."Most kids, they live on social media," the chief said. "Everything they do is based on social media and TikTok and likes and things of that nature."The department has created an internal team to monitor social media activity that could impact Riviera Beach and surrounding areas, he said.The chief urged parents to closely monitor their children’s behavior and not to obstruct police if they know their kids are involved in illegal activity."Don't protect your kids and interfere with law enforcement investigations," he said. "Then you put yourself in a situation where you may be brought up on criminal charges as well."Standing alongside police, Pastor Drayton of St. James — a longtime community leader who has worked on anti-violence efforts in Riviera Beach — said the killing has left the community “bruised and damaged,” but not beyond hope."We pledge to do all that we can to make certain that this doesn’t happen again," he said. "Because we're bruised and damaged doesn’t mean that we're at the point of no return."He praised the police department for "following due process and getting those responsible" and said faith leaders and community groups will continue working with law enforcement to help the neighborhood heal and prevent further violence.City officials emphasized that despite the homicide, they want residents and visitors to view Riviera Beach as a safe place to live, work and visit."This is something that we’ve got to deal with every single day with violence throughout the country," the chief said. "But Riviera Beach is a place that I consider a great place, and I want everybody outside of Riviera Beach to feel it’s a great place to come and enjoy the beaches that we have in our communities."As of the news conference, the three juveniles were being held at the Juvenile Assessment Center in Palm Beach County. Whether they will ultimately be charged as adults will be determined by state prosecutors and the courts, officials said.Anyone with information about the shooting is urged to contact Riviera Beach police or speak with investigators.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Tom Poidevin has been a WPTV Weather Spotter since the beginning. Here's why he joined.
entry.summary: Tom Poidevin of Lake Worth has been part of the WPTV Weather Spotter Program since the very beginning and his passion for weather goes back even further than that. 'I saw the early commercials on the channel and it really interested me,' Poidevin said. He was among the first to sign up, even visiting the station for an introductory session when the program launched. Poidevin also has a secret weapon when it comes to tracking incoming storms: his dog, Eden. 'We call her weather dog, because she's usually about 5 minutes ahead of the storm where she knows what's coming,' Poidevin said. His interest in weather stretches back to his years in New York, where he grew up watching storms roll in from the mountains. He said South Florida's weather patterns offer a completely different experience. 'I've always been interested in weather when I was in New York. entry.title: 15-year-old student arrested after false bomb threat at Martin County High School - cw34.com
entry.summary: 15-year-old student arrested after false bomb threat at Martin County High School    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old student was arrested Tuesday after threatening Martin County High School , according to the district. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. The threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district. Investigators with the Martin County Sheriff's Office said school resource officers and Criminal Investigations Division detectives traced the message back to Taylor. During the investigation, Taylor confessed to sending the threat, according to the Sheriff's Office. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The threat was reported through FortifyFL, Principal Lori Vogel previously told families. The Sheriff's Office immediately began investigating and identified the apparent source of the message. The district notified families Tuesday that an arrest had been made after initially telling parents an arrest appeared imminent. The Sheriff's Office said the arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks. Investigators said they can only link Taylor to this specific threat. School officials said students found to have been involved in making threats could face both school disciplinary action and legal consequences. The district also reminded families that FortifyFL is an important tool for reporting legitimate safety concerns, but knowingly submitting false information or making a false threat can have serious consequences. False threats are neither harmless nor funny, Vogel said, adding that they can cause fear, disrupt learning, and place a burden on students, families, school employees, and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said threats made anonymously, through text messages, online, or through other electronic communications, can still be traced and investigated.

entry.article_text: At Hillcrest Memorial Gardens, Marc Raczkoski stares painfully at a place he's often tried to avoid. "Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff's department, Indian River County," reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. WATCH BELOW: Brother finally gets closure as Florida deputy killer's execution date setIt's the grave of his older brother, who was just 29 years old when he was buried at the Fort Pierce cemetery. "I was 22," Marc said quietly. "I was 22." It's always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that's brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there." entry.title: 3 teens arrested in connection to deadly shooting of 17-year-old girl in Riviera Beach
entry.summary: Three minors have been arrested in connection with the fatal shooting of a 17-year-old girl in Riviera Beach, according to the Riviera Beach Police Department. The U.S. Marshals Service took the suspects into custody for the Aug. 21 shooting, and all three now face first-degree murder charges. Riviera Beach Police Chief Michael A. Coleman held a press conference Tuesday morning to provide more details on the case. 'This was a heartbreaking loss for her family, her friends, and our community,' Coleman said. 'According to our investigation, three juveniles allegedly planned to rob the victim of a firearm she attempted to sell. That attempted robbery escalated into violence, and a young life was cut short.' entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - WPEC
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Boca Raton golfer Frankie Harris aims for PGA Tour after record-setting college career
entry.summary: Boca Raton native Frankie Harris is making a name for himself in professional golf, winning a Korn Ferry Tour title just months into his pro career and setting his sights on the PGA Tour. Harris grew up with golf in his blood. His father was a professional golfer, and Harris had a club in his hands almost from birth. WATCH BELOW: Boca Raton golfer sets sights on PGA Tour Boca Raton golfer sets sights on PGA Tour 'I had a golf club in my hands at a very young age. My father was a professional golfer,' Harris said. He began his golf journey around age 8, quickly making a name for himself as a junior golfer. 'I stacked up a lot of wins as a junior golfer. I've kind of always known deep down that I had something pretty special,' Harris said. Harris went on to win several national and local tournaments before entering high school at Boca Raton, where he discovered a new dimension of the game. 'Golf is an individual sport, so having teammates and playing for something bigger than yourself was something pretty interesting to me,' Harris said. His dominance continued at the high school level, where he won regionals, qualified for state and earned player of the year honors. After one year at Auburn, Harris transferred to the University of South Carolina, where he built a dynasty, setting school records over his college career. 'To stack up six wins throughout my career, there was definitely a special thing,' Harris said. After graduating, Harris turned pro and wasted no time making an impact. He won a Korn Ferry Tour title just months into his professional career, shooting a historic round in the process. 'Kind of reached my flow state. I never shot a 59 before, and I was fortunate to do that on Sunday,' Harris said. His 12-under 59 secured the title and put him on a fast track toward the PGA Tour. Harris said returning to Broken Sound in southern Palm Beach County, where his golf journey began, carries special meaning. 'It's always great being back in South Florida; it's my favorite place in the world; it's somewhere where I want to stay the rest of my life,' Harris said.

entry.article_text: Jennifer Eckhart, a popular podcaster and former associate producer at Fox Business, died by suicide at her home in Hobe Sound on Saturday morning, according to the Martin County sheriff. Sheriff John Budensiek said he usually doesn't comment on suicides but decided to speak publicly about Eckhart’s death to address conspiracy theories suggesting she had been murdered. "Looking at the scene and going through the investigation, we spent a lot of time. We investigated it as if it was a homicide. Unfortunately, she took her life at her own hands," Budensiek said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Eckhart gained notoriety after accusing a Fox News anchor of raping her. Investigators said she had family and friends who tried to help her, but she had been in and out of mental health facilities and had stopped taking her medications. If you'd like to talk to someone at 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast, you can dial 211. If you'd like to text the helpline, you can message your ZIP code to 898211. Elizabeth Burrows, director of development and communications with 211 Palm Beach and Treasure Coast, emphasized the tragedy of suicide and encouraged those struggling to seek help. "Every death by suicide is a tragedy," Burrows said. She noted that anyone in crisis can call 211 or 988, which are available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, to provide resources or someone to talk to. "You'd be surprised at how often just having someone who's there to listen can help someone make it through their darkest moments," Burrows said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Burrows also stressed the importance of being present and asking questions when supporting someone who may be struggling. Asking about it does not make suicide more of a risk for them. If anything, it lets that person know that they are not alone," she said. "The one answer I can always give is to never give up. As long as someone is still here, there is still an opportunity to support and assist them." The sheriff said Eckhart’s death remains an open investigation as they await toxicology results, but he emphasized that all evidence points to suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available by dialing 211 or 988 for confidential support and resources. If you or someone you know needs help, you can talk with the Suicide Crisis Lifeline by calling or sending a text message to 988, or you can chat online here.

entry.title: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old student is facing a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat targeting Martin County High School Tuesday morning. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the student later admitted he made the threat because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. According to investigators, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL , a school safety reporting system, around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. During a news conference, Sheriff John Budensiek read the message that prompted the investigation. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," the sheriff read. The sheriff said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating. Authorities say surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. According to an affidavit, another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students. However, deputies said he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. According to Budensiek, Taylor later explained why he made the threat. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class." Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The arrest comes amid a string of bomb threats tied to Martin County High School. The sheriff said this is the fourth threat connected to the campus in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating, the sheriff added. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation. In a statement, Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact false threats can have on a school community. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek also warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences. "This individual has now been arrested, charged with a felony, getting expelled from school, likely. Getting a job down in the future is going to be very difficult for them because of the type of threat it is. These things that students think are funny can have long-term repercussions." The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

I spent a lot of time there on my lunch breaks for work, and I know that the property taxes pay for a significant amount of the upkeep, the maintenance, stuff like that," Mroczkowski said. "I'm a big fan of when taxes are utilized to better the community."While acknowledging the referendum could save him money personally, Mroczkowski said he currently plans to vote against it."I am personally of the opinion that I'm probably going to vote no on the referendum. I know it could save me money, but unselfishly, I think it's more important that those taxes are used to better the community," Mroczkowski said.Jacks said the potential impact stretches far beyond individual homeowners.According to Jacks, that equates to roughly "$324 million in tax revenue that would go away."She noted that's only the county's share."And that's just the county. There's certainly many other taxing authorities that would also see similar reductions," Jacks said.The new calculator is designed to help residents understand both sides of that equation."We also wanted people to understand the two sides to Amendment 3, the one side that yes, I, as a homesteader, would save more, but also there's an impact to the many taxing authorities that each of us pay and to sort of share with them what that impact would be when you start bundling together 300,000 homesteads in Palm Beach County, not just my own," Jacks said.Residents with a homestead exemption can simply enter their address to generate an estimate."You would just put your address into this field here and then of course it just goes down and gives you the data," Jacks explained.The calculator will show current estimated taxes, projected changes for 2027 and 2028 if Amendment 3 passes, and estimated revenue impacts to local taxing districts.Jacks said the system will also indicate if a property does not have a homestead exemption and therefore is not eligible for the proposed tax benefit.The projections are based on 2026 certified property values and millage rates.She cautioned that future tax bills could still vary."That depends on the millage rates, which can change. entry.title: Spam calls and texts are a growing problem — but there's a way to reduce them
entry.summary: Spam calls and text messages are a frustration shared by millions of people, and one local man says the problem has gotten out of hand. Recently, I heard from Mark Shubert about the unwanted calls he was getting every day. WATCH BELOW: How you can reduce those annoying spam calls, texts Tips for Ending Robo Calls 'Really very infuriating; that's why I contacted you because I didn't know where to turn,' Shubert said. He said he's been getting over 30 calls a day for the last couple of months. The calls come from different area codes, and usually with the same type of computer-generated voice, making a pitch to sign up for Medicare-related programs. 'You're supposed to think it's somebody live youre talking to, and it's not,' he says. Making the calls stop is not easy, but there are things we can do. 'I was starting to just receive an alarming number of calls,' says Kim Key, senior security writer at PC Mag. Key recently wrote an article about the ways she found to put a stop to the calls, and it usually starts in the settings of your phone. 'If you find something that says silence unknown callers, you're on the right track,' Key said. 'There are also other settings that can block unknown numbers from sending you texts.' Several carriers also offer call screening and scanning to filter calls. Key said the best option to act so telemarketers and scammers don't have access to your number. 'Get right in there and get your information, as much of it as you can, off of the public web,' she said. 'And that means going to a data broker website like Whitepages.com, like Spokeo, and requesting to have your information removed. It is free. It takes 5 minutes. That is what cut my spam calls in half when I did that.'

entry.article_text: At Hillcrest Memorial Gardens, Marc Raczkoski stares painfully at a place he's often tried to avoid. "Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff's department, Indian River County," reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. WATCH BELOW: Brother finally gets closure as Florida deputy killer's execution date setIt's the grave of his older brother, who was just 29 years old when he was buried at the Fort Pierce cemetery. "I was 22," Marc said quietly. "I was 22." It's always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that's brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there." entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. entry.title: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law?    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: A proposed luxury waterfront development in Fort Pierce is drawing renewed attention after city commissioners approved a motion to explore hiring outside legal counsel to review whether the city has any options to challenge the project under Florida's Live Local Act. 14 vote comes as cities across Florida continue testing the limits of the state's Live Local Act and lawmakers implement the latest round of changes to the law. The proposed Causeway Cove development on South Hutchinson Island has become one of the Treasure Coast's most closely watched growth disputes, putting residents and local officials at odds with a state law that limits how much control cities have over certain housing projects. 14 meeting, the commission approved a motion to explore hiring an outside land-use attorney to determine whether Fort Pierce has any legal grounds to challenge the project under the Live Local Act. The city is also monitoring lawsuits filed elsewhere in Florida that seek to restore greater local control over development decisions. The move comes as Florida enters the latest phase of the law. Known as Live Local 4.0, the most recent changes took effect July 1, 2026, expanding eligible development sites and further clarifying protections for qualifying projects that include affordable housing. Qualifying developments must continue to reserve at least 40% of units as affordable rental housing for at least 30 years. Now, Fort Pierce finds itself at the center of a broader statewide debate over growth, affordable housing and home rule. The proposed redevelopment would dramatically transform the Causeway Cove property along Seaway Drive. According to city records, plans call for five towers ranging from 11 to 17 stories, 913 residential units, two hotels totaling 407 rooms, more than 72,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, and 218 marina slips. For residents like Edie Harrison, the project would change the area known for its waterfront views, boating access and small-town character. "Everything is still very quaint," Harrison said. "It's one of those gems." Harrison and hundreds of other residents have raised concerns about the size of the development, traffic impacts and what they view as a lack of public input. At the center of the fight is Florida's Live Local Act, a law passed in 2023 to encourage the construction of affordable and workforce housing across the state. The law allows qualifying projects to bypass certain local zoning, density and height restrictions if affordability requirements are met. City officials have repeatedly said the proposed Causeway Cove project qualifies under the law and therefore moves through an administrative review process rather than a traditional public hearing and commission vote. For critics, that process has become one of the most controversial aspects of the proposal. Fort Pierce Commissioner Michael Broderick said residents' concerns extend beyond the size of the development. "The concern is density, traffic flow," Broderick said, pointing to longstanding concerns about capacity on Seaway Drive. Another major debate centers on affordability. Under Live Local, affordable housing calculations are based on regional income levels rather than income levels specific to Fort Pierce. Critics argue the formula can produce rents that technically qualify as affordable under state guidelines but remain difficult for many local residents to afford. According to city officials, some qualifying units could rent for more than $2,300 per month, while Fort Pierce's median rent is substantially lower. Broderick said many residents question whether those figures reflect true affordability within the city. Even some lawmakers who supported the legislation have raised concerns about how it is being applied. Dana Trabulsy, whose district includes parts of the Treasure Coast, has recently questioned whether developments of this scale reflect what legislators intended when they approved the measure. The Fort Pierce dispute is also part of a much larger battle unfolding across Florida. Several lawsuits challenging aspects of the Live Local Act are moving through the courts as cities seek to regain greater authority over local development decisions. Supporters of the law argue it is helping address Florida's housing shortage, while critics contend it has weakened local home-rule powers and limited communities' ability to shape growth. Land-use attorney Keith Poliakoff, who has represented clients in Live Local disputes across the state, said local governments generally have limited discretion once a project satisfies state requirements. Poliakoff said the law effectively requires municipalities to administratively approve qualifying projects, even when residents or local leaders oppose the density, height or scale of a development. State data show more than 200 Live Local projects have been proposed or approved across Florida , making the law one of the most significant growth and housing measures enacted in recent years. Related 2024 article: $100M Kanner Hwy development in Stuart: Affordable housing powered by Live Local Act If things move forward as anticipated, construction on the Causeway Cove development could begin before the end of the year. The property's owner, Palm Beach developer Ashton DePeyster, did not respond to requests for comment. This report is part of an ongoing CBS12 News I-Team investigation examining the impact of Florida's Live Local Act, the legal challenges surrounding the law, and how communities across the Treasure Coast are responding to large-scale development projects.

entry.title: 'Nobody can see what I do to you': New report details alleged Port St. Lucie MRI assault - cbs12.com
entry.summary: 'Nobody can see what I do to you': New report details alleged Port St. Lucie MRI assault    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital allegedly told her, Nobody can see what I can do to you, before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a Port St. CBS12 News previously reported the arrest of Gabriel Cruz, 42, a traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. He faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. "In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. The criminal complaint says on Sept. 14, shortly after 8 a.m., officers responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital after a patient reported that a technician had sexually assaulted her, the report states. Officers met with the hospital’s director of patient safety, who said the patient reported being sexually assaulted by a male Hispanic imaging technician during the time of her MRI. The patient told investigators that Spanish is her primary language and that she had been admitted to the hospital after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 According to the report, the patient was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. She said medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt. The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states that he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel. Another person later transported the patient back to her room. Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August, according to the report. "Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time. We spoke with a local rape crisis counselor about the impact of something like this. "It is a very confusing time for people. It can bring upon people feeling ashamed, they can feel fearful, confused, guilty, angry. They can have difficulty relating with people close to them after the fact," said Julie Stoyka, Director, Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee. Their rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital. But, you know, truly you're not safe anywhere," Chief Niemczyk said. Lucie Hospital released a statement that says: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical - WFLX
entry.summary: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon. Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting. The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911. Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris’ waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris’ front pocket, police said. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm. Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital. No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

entry.title: X-ray technician accused of sexually assaulting patient during MRI at HCA St. Lucie Hospital
entry.summary: A traveling X-ray technician has been accused of sexually assaulting a patient during an MRI procedure at HCA St. Lucie Medical Hospital, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. Gabriel Cruz, 42, of Grant-Valkaria, was working as a contract technician at the hospital when the alleged assault occurred on Sept. 13. The victim, a female patient who was receiving treatment for fainting episodes, reported the incident to hospital administration the following day. According to the police report, the patient had been brought to the emergency room by her nephew on Sept. 11 for evaluation after experiencing fainting spells and head injuries. She underwent a CT scan and was scheduled for an MRI two days later to further assess her condition. The victim told investigators that Cruz made inappropriate comments before the procedure, allegedly telling her 'nobody can see what I can do to you.' During the MRI, the patient was given medication that made her drowsy. She reported waking up to find Cruz sexually assaulting her. Hospital security footage from Sept. 13 shows Cruz entering the MRI room with the patient and later exiting while carrying an unknown object and wearing purple latex gloves. The video confirms Cruz was the only person in the MRI room with the victim during the time period in question. According to the police report, Cruz had been working at the hospital on contract since August 2026. The case has been forwarded to the Criminal Investigation Division for further investigation. WPTV received this statement from HCA St. Lucie Medical Hospital on Sept. 17: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individuals assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

entry.title: Peloton is releasing its cheapest treadmill yet as it bets on running for a turnaround
entry.summary: Peloton is launching its cheapest treadmill yet, in the hope that runnings surging popularity will spur sales. The fitness equipment maker announced Tuesday it will soon release a $2,195 treadmill called the Tread Flex. Thats about $1,000 cheaper than its current lineup, and also the companys first-ever foldable device that contracts to roughly half its size. Peloton hopes the space-saving design will entice new customers, like those with apartments or smaller homes, to buy the companys pricey equipment. Focusing on walking and running is a major initiative for CEO Peter Stern, who has the massive task of transforming the beleaguered company. Once a pandemic-era success story, sales have slumped in recent years and its stock has fallen 42% since it last unveiled new products, in October 2025. That equipment ultimately failed to lure back shoppers and the company conducted another round of layoffs at the beginning of the year. entry.title: 'I'm not going back to prison': New details emerge in Palm City SWAT standoff - cbs12.com
entry.summary: 'I'm not going back to prison': New details emerge in Palm City SWAT standoff    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Before an hours-long SWAT standoff in Palm City , a man allegedly threatened to kill himself and his ex-girlfriend after she went to his home to check on him following their breakup, a new report reveals. According to an arrest report from the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the ex-girlfriend of the suspect, Darrel Abbey, arrived at his home at about 12:08 p.m. after the two had broken up the previous night. She told investigators Abbey was not doing well mentally and had previously made comments about killing himself. When she arrived, Abbey had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts, according to the report. The woman told investigators Abbey appeared to be extremely intoxicated. The arrest report says Abbey brought both firearms inside the home and began screaming at the woman, "I should die, you should kill me," while holding a gun. Investigators said Abbey continued yelling at the woman while recording the interaction on his phone. The woman told investigators that Abbey pointed the gun at her several times and threatened to kill her and her stepfather. At one point, Abbey allegedly placed the gun under his chin and pulled the trigger, but the firearm did not discharge because the magazine had been removed, according to the report. Investigators said Abbey later began packing his vehicle. Fearing he was going to shoot her stepfather, the woman took the gun away from him, but Abbey allegedly continued reaching for it as she begged him to stop. The report says that when Abbey picked up the gun again, he said, "This is really f***** dangerous now." Investigators said Abbey continued drinking bourbon and Jameson throughout the encounter. As Abbey walked outside, the woman told investigators she heard several loud "pop" sounds. Abbey then returned inside to retrieve a rifle and allegedly tried to get the woman to come outside and shoot it with him. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? When she asked what he was shooting at, Abbey allegedly told her he had hung a bucket from a nearby tree and was shooting at it. At some point during the incident, Abbey allegedly began cleaning the firearms and said, "I gotta wipe all my fingerprints off, I gotta get the gunshot residue off of my hands, I'm not going back to prison." The report says Abbey later attempted to get into his vehicle while continuing to drink, prompting the woman to begin recording him. Investigators who reviewed the video said Abbey appeared intoxicated while sitting in the driver's seat, slurred his words and struggled to hold his head upright. When Abbey realized the woman was recording, he allegedly reached for her phone. The woman then ran down the road until a passing motorist stopped to help her. Deputies later attempted to contact Abbey at the residence, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, leading to an hours-long standoff involving the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and hostage negotiators. Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. Investigators also said Abbey is a convicted felon from Washington state with a prior conviction for vehicular assault.

entry.title: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation - WPBF
entry.summary: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie road rage fight ends in shooting, 2 men arrested, police say    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Lucie road rage incident that escalated into a physical fight and shooting landed two men in handcuffs Thursday. Lucie Police Department, the incident happened at about 6:30 p.m. near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace. Police said that before the shooting, one driver believed he was being followed after merging onto Southwest Crosstown Parkway. The vehicles had passed each other, and one driver believed the other had cut him off. Investigators determined there was no intentional following, police said. One of the drivers, identified as Tylon Kukielka, 57, was driving with his girlfriend to her home after leaving a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as Dean Plotts, 41, was traveling in the same direction. Police said the situation escalated into a physical fight near Southwest Brevity Terrace, when Plotts got out of his truck and confronted Kukielka's car. "He got out of his vehicle and approached the other vehicle, which was parked in front of him, and he approached it, and he punched the driver of that vehicle through the open window," said Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk. See also: Formerly conjoined twins see each other face-to-face after historic separation surgery Investigators say Plotts went back to his own vehicle, but Kukielka followed with a gun and shot him multiple times. While an arrest report indicates the two men were facing each other when the shots were fired, Niemczyk said Plotts wasn't confronting Kukielka again he was trying to get away. "The reason they were facing the same direction is because he was turning to his open car door, [trying] to get back in his vehicle," Niemczyk said. "So he wasn't actually going back to confront [him]." A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy traveling in the area witnessed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also taken to a hospital for a medical evaluation. Investigators recovered surveillance video and shell casings during the investigation. Detectives later charged Kukielka with attempted homicide. Plotts was charged with burglary with assault or battery a charge Niemczyk said surprises people unfamiliar with the statute. "Most people will associate that with a house or a business," Niemczyk said. "But you can also commit burglary of a conveyance, which is a vehicle. So by punching the individual, he broke the plane of that vehicle." The incident remains under investigation. Niemczyk said road rage incidents like this one have become more common in Port St. "I would say over the last few years, yeah, we've had quite a few road rage incidents in this city," Niemczyk said. "And obviously with the increased volume of traffic in the community and the congestion that a lot of our residents are accustomed to, frustration comes along with that."

entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Family seeks answers after pre-purchased burial plot in Delray Beach cemetery was sold to someone else
entry.summary: A Delray Beach family is demanding accountability from the city after discovering that a burial plot they had purchased years ago at the Delray Beach Municipal Cemetery was sold and used to bury someone else. The discovery has caused significant heartbreak for Delila Kellum and her family, who were unable to fulfill her father's final wish to be buried next to his brother. 'It's just heartbreak; it's upsetting,' Kellum told WPTV. 'We can't bury him where he wanted, so we havent really decided what to do.' WPTV's Zitlali Solache has been covering multiple concerns involving the cemetery's overcapacity , maintenance , and record-keeping , pressing the city for answers. WATCH: Family seeks answers after pre-purchased burial plot was sold to someone else Delray Beach family demands answers after burial plot mix-up A painful discovery The issue began in 2010 when Kellum and her sister took their father to visit his late brother's grave. Their parents had purchased two adjacent plots. 'When we took him to there, we got out and looked at the stone and when we look over... we noticed somebody was buried in my mothers spot,' Kellum said. The family immediately contacted the city but were told the body could not be moved. According to Kellum, a supervisor offered them two different plots and promised to provide new deeds. 'To this day we've never seen them,' Kellum said. 'My sister tried to contact them when my father passed, but nothing.' When her father died in 2024, the family was faced with a devastating reality. 'We couldn't put him in his spot next to his brother, we had to get him cremated,' she explained, adding they skipped a proper funeral. Kellum said her mother suffers from dementia and is unaware of the distressing situation. 'Now were just gonna wait for my mother to pass and have it together,' she said. A history of problems This is not the first time the Kellum family has encountered issues with the cemetery's record-keeping. Kellum said they have also struggled to locate the grave of her grandfather, a Pearl Harbor veteran. Although the city initially denied he was buried there, Kellum stated that funeral home officials provided documents proving his interment at the Delray Beach Municipal Cemetery. 'We went to go try to find him and we couldn't find him,' she said. The family has documents, including a deed from 1994, which they believe prove their ownership of the original plots. entry.title: Martin County High student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says
entry.summary: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he 'was just tired of being in class,' according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.
