entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. entry.title: Police: Three Fort Pierce shootings that hit homes are connected and targeted - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Police: Three Fort Pierce shootings that hit homes are connected and targeted    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18 according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

entry.title: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation - WPBF
entry.summary: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - cw34.com
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Semi-truck fire shuts down SW Pratt Whitney Road near South Fork High School
entry.summary: A semi tractor-trailer fire has forced a closure of a major roadway in Stuart, affecting traffic flow and school access Wednesday morning. SW Pratt Whitney Road is completely closed from just south of SW Bulldog Way to Bridge Road as emergency crews respond to the incident. The closure is impacting access to South Fork High School, with only students and staff able to reach the campus from the northern approach. No injuries have been reported at this time, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation. Motorists are urged to avoid the area entirely and seek alternate routes. The closure is expected to remain in effect until the scene is cleared and the roadway is deemed safe for travel.

entry.title: Martin County High student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County High student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half.WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threatThe arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.Martin County Sheriff Jon Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday."The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus.When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement."Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip."However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said.While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school."The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case."Sheriff Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke."This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. entry.article_text: At Hillcrest Memorial Gardens, Marc Raczkoski stares painfully at a place he's often tried to avoid. "Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff's department, Indian River County," reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there." entry.summary: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. entry.article_text: A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital allegedly told her, Nobody can see what I can do to you, before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a Port St. CBS12 News previously reported the arrest of Gabriel Cruz, 42, a traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. He faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. "In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. The criminal complaint says on Sept. 14, shortly after 8 a.m., officers responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital after a patient reported that a technician had sexually assaulted her, the report states. Officers met with the hospital’s director of patient safety, who said the patient reported being sexually assaulted by a male Hispanic imaging technician during the time of her MRI. The patient told investigators that Spanish is her primary language and that she had been admitted to the hospital after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 According to the report, the patient was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. She said medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt. The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states that he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel. Another person later transported the patient back to her room. Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August, according to the report. "Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time. We spoke with a local rape crisis counselor about the impact of something like this. "It is a very confusing time for people. It can bring upon people feeling ashamed, they can feel fearful, confused, guilty, angry. They can have difficulty relating with people close to them after the fact," said Julie Stoyka, Director, Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee. Their rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital. But, you know, truly you're not safe anywhere," Chief Niemczyk said. Lucie Hospital released a statement that says: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County
entry.summary: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m. Wednesday morning.

entry.title: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old student is facing a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat targeting Martin County High School Tuesday morning. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the student later admitted he made the threat because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. According to investigators, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL , a school safety reporting system, around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. During a news conference, Sheriff John Budensiek read the message that prompted the investigation. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," the sheriff read. The sheriff said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating. Authorities say surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. According to an affidavit, another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students. However, deputies said he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. According to Budensiek, Taylor later explained why he made the threat. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class." Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The arrest comes amid a string of bomb threats tied to Martin County High School. The sheriff said this is the fourth threat connected to the campus in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating, the sheriff added. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation. In a statement, Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact false threats can have on a school community. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek also warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences. "This individual has now been arrested, charged with a felony, getting expelled from school, likely. Getting a job down in the future is going to be very difficult for them because of the type of threat it is. These things that students think are funny can have long-term repercussions." The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    WPEC
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - WPBF
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. Each threat is taken seriously and requires a significant response from law enforcement and emergency personnel, regardless of whether the threat ultimately proves to be a hoax,” the sheriff’s office said. It added that the suspect was only linked to the threat to the high school on Tuesday, Sept. “The Sheriff’s Office will thoroughly investigate these incidents and aggressively pursue those responsible when the investigation provides sufficient evidence to identify them. entry.summary: Martin County High student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half. WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threat The arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks. Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus. When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement. "Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip." However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said. While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school. "The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case." Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke. "This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious." This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - cw34.com
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: 'Nobody can see what I do to you': New report details alleged Port St. Lucie MRI assault - WPEC
entry.summary: 'Nobody can see what I do to you': New report details alleged Port St. Lucie MRI assault    WPEC
entry.article_text: A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital allegedly told her, Nobody can see what I can do to you, before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a Port St. CBS12 News previously reported the arrest of Gabriel Cruz, 42, a traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. He faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. "In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. The criminal complaint says on Sept. 14, shortly after 8 a.m., officers responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital after a patient reported that a technician had sexually assaulted her, the report states. Officers met with the hospital’s director of patient safety, who said the patient reported being sexually assaulted by a male Hispanic imaging technician during the time of her MRI. The patient told investigators that Spanish is her primary language and that she had been admitted to the hospital after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 According to the report, the patient was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. She said medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt. The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states that he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel. Another person later transported the patient back to her room. Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August, according to the report. "Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time. We spoke with a local rape crisis counselor about the impact of something like this. "It is a very confusing time for people. It can bring upon people feeling ashamed, they can feel fearful, confused, guilty, angry. They can have difficulty relating with people close to them after the fact," said Julie Stoyka, Director, Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee. Their rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital. But, you know, truly you're not safe anywhere," Chief Niemczyk said. Lucie Hospital released a statement that says: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

entry.title: Fort Pierce home hit by gunfire, bullet enters child's bedroom - cw34.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce home hit by gunfire, bullet enters child's bedroom    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18 according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

entry.article_text: With just weeks to go before voters decide the fate of Amendment 3, one of the most talked-about questions across Palm Beach County remains the same: What does it mean for my wallet?WPTV has been following the debate for months as county leaders, residents and taxpayers weigh the potential benefits and drawbacks of the controversial property tax proposal that will appear on the November ballot.WATCH BELOW: Amendment 3 calculator to launch in Palm Beach CountyNow, Palm Beach County homeowners have a new tool aimed at answering that question with personalized numbers."We're excited to launch the Amendment 3 calculator, which will let residents, homesteaded residents, actually look up their own property and find out what their taxes could be after Amendment 3 passes, should it pass," Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks said.The new online Amendment 3 calculator allows homesteaded property owners to enter their address and see an estimate of how the proposed constitutional amendment could affect their property taxes, along with the potential revenue impact on local taxing authorities.Amendment 3 has become a regular topic at county meetings as officials discuss their budgets and what could happen if voters approve the measure.The amendment requires at least 60% voter approval on Nov. According to the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser's Office, the exemption could increase to as much as $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School taxes would not receive the same increase.Supporters argue it would provide much-needed tax relief for homeowners dealing with rising costs."I plan to vote to eliminate property taxes," said Gillian Lieberman, a Palm Beach County property owner and real estate professional. "People work hard, and I think everyone that I work with, my colleagues, my friends, my clients, they work hard, and I'd like them to see that money back in their pocket as much as possible."Lieberman said she believes property owners could use the savings."We have such a great city, great infrastructure, great development, and I don't think eliminating property taxes is going to hurt that. I think it's going to allow owners to do more and purchase more so they have less stress when the tax bill comes," she said.Others are concerned about the potential loss of funding for community services.Logan Mroczkowski, a Palm Beach County homeowner, pointed to local parks and public amenities that benefit from property tax revenue."I work in Lake Worth, and I spent a lot of time at Bryant Park. I spent a lot of time there on my lunch breaks for work, and I know that the property taxes pay for a significant amount of the upkeep, the maintenance, stuff like that," Mroczkowski said. "I'm a big fan of when taxes are utilized to better the community."While acknowledging the referendum could save him money personally, Mroczkowski said he currently plans to vote against it."I am personally of the opinion that I'm probably going to vote no on the referendum. I know it could save me money, but unselfishly, I think it's more important that those taxes are used to better the community," Mroczkowski said.Jacks said the potential impact stretches far beyond individual homeowners.According to Jacks, that equates to roughly "$324 million in tax revenue that would go away."She noted that's only the county's share."And that's just the county. There's certainly many other taxing authorities that would also see similar reductions," Jacks said.The new calculator is designed to help residents understand both sides of that equation."We also wanted people to understand the two sides to Amendment 3, the one side that yes, I, as a homesteader, would save more, but also there's an impact to the many taxing authorities that each of us pay and to sort of share with them what that impact would be when you start bundling together 300,000 homesteads in Palm Beach County, not just my own," Jacks said.Residents with a homestead exemption can simply enter their address to generate an estimate."You would just put your address into this field here and then of course it just goes down and gives you the data," Jacks explained.The calculator will show current estimated taxes, projected changes for 2027 and 2028 if Amendment 3 passes, and estimated revenue impacts to local taxing districts.Jacks said the system will also indicate if a property does not have a homestead exemption and therefore is not eligible for the proposed tax benefit.The projections are based on 2026 certified property values and millage rates.She cautioned that future tax bills could still vary."That depends on the millage rates, which can change. They could go up, and it also depends on their value, which also could go up," Jacks said.Because the calculator uses parcel-level data, Jacks believes it can offer a clearer picture than broad statewide estimates."I think because we're able to do it at the parcel level, so individually, it's probably one of the more accurate," Jacks said.The tool also accounts for local differences."Absolutely, that's the point," Jacks said when asked whether results will vary depending on where someone lives. It's what you're paying."Jacks emphasized that the Property Appraiser's Office is not advocating for or against the amendment."It's really here to educate and nothing more," Jacks said.Instead, she hopes the calculator gives residents a way to move beyond campaign rhetoric and evaluate the proposal based on their own situation."So often these amendments appear on the ballot, and there isn't really a tool or a resource you can go to to say OK, well, how is that going to affect me and we thought this would be a good way to do that," Jacks said.Ultimately, she said, the goal is simple."We're hoping that the public will say, wow, you know, OK, let me look at my numbers and let me make a decision based on my numbers as opposed to all this chatter going on," Jacks said.For Palm Beach County voters still deciding how they'll cast their ballot in November, that personalized look may arrive just in time.The Amendment 3 Homestead Calculator is live now on the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser's website.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Florida GOP redraw faces new questions as Democrats defend Castor and ratings shift
entry.summary: National Democrats are spending to defend U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor as seven Florida congressional races shift toward their party in new ratings, renewing debate over whether Republicans mid-decade redraw will deliver its intended gains. The map targeted as many as four additional Republican seats . Democrats have called it a potential dummymander a partisan redraw that backfires on the party that designed it. The spending puts national party resources behind an incumbent Republicans targeted with the new boundaries. Inside Elections moved Castors race to a toss-up on Sept. 17 , following an earlier shift from lean Republican to tilt Republican. The forecaster rated the district solid Democratic before the redraw, underscoring how much more competitive her reelection contest has become. The latest changes extend beyond Tampa.
