entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - wpbf.com
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. The letter says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." The letter goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead.

entry.title: Amendment 3 could shift property-tax costs onto Florida renters, report warns
entry.summary: A tax break for Florida homeowners could bring a bigger bill for renters next door, according to a new report examining Amendment 3. The report released by the Florida Housing Coalition estimates that if local governments raise property-tax rates to replace revenue lost under the amendment, annual taxes would increase by an average of $406 per apartment and $1,081 per single-family rental home in 2028. Watch more from Forrest Saunders on the report Amendment 3 could shift property-tax costs onto Florida renters, report warns Much of that expense could ultimately be passed on to tenants through higher rents, said Jared Walczak, the tax-policy analyst who wrote the report. Renters pay taxes, they just don't write the check, Walczak said. Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The exemption reduces the property value on which taxes are calculated for qualifying primary residences. School district property taxes would remain unchanged. Rental properties do not qualify for the homestead exemption. Local governments facing lost revenue could respond by cutting spending, increasing property-tax rates, raising other taxes or fees, or combining those approaches. Walczaks analysis models rate increases intended to replace lost revenue, subject to existing limits on those rates. While landlords would write the check, most of the burden would ultimately be borne by renters in the form of higher rent, he said. The estimates represent average increases in property-tax bills. How much of that cost reaches tenants would depend on rental-market conditions and local budget decisions. By 2031, the report estimates the additional annual property-tax burden would reach $544 per apartment and $1,471 per single-family rental home under the same approach. The amendment also includes a provision benefiting rental and other non-homestead properties: It would lower the annual cap on increases in assessed value from 10% to 5%. That limits assessment growth, while allowing local tax rates to rise. Walczaks report concludes that the benefit of the lower assessment cap would be outweighed by the modeled tax shift. Supporters, including Florida Realtors, argue that homeowners also need help with housing costs. Everywhere you look, people are feeling the pinch of affordability, and Amendment 3 has the opportunity to return more money back to the taxpayer, said
entry.article_text: A tax break for Florida homeowners could bring a bigger bill for renters next door, according to a new report examining Amendment 3.The report released by the Florida Housing Coalition estimates that if local governments raise property-tax rates to replace revenue lost under the amendment, annual taxes would increase by an average of $406 per apartment and $1,081 per single-family rental home in 2028.Watch more from Forrest Saunders on the reportMuch of that expense could ultimately be passed on to tenants through higher rents, said Jared Walczak, the tax-policy analyst who wrote the report.“Renters pay taxes, they just don't write the check,” Walczak said.Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The exemption reduces the property value on which taxes are calculated for qualifying primary residences. School district property taxes would remain unchanged.Rental properties do not qualify for the homestead exemption.Local governments facing lost revenue could respond by cutting spending, increasing property-tax rates, raising other taxes or fees, or combining those approaches. Walczak’s analysis models rate increases intended to replace lost revenue, subject to existing limits on those rates.“While landlords would write the check, most of the burden would ultimately be borne by renters in the form of higher rent,” he said.The estimates represent average increases in property-tax bills. How much of that cost reaches tenants would depend on rental-market conditions and local budget decisions.By 2031, the report estimates the additional annual property-tax burden would reach $544 per apartment and $1,471 per single-family rental home under the same approach.The amendment also includes a provision benefiting rental and other non-homestead properties: It would lower the annual cap on increases in assessed value from 10% to 5%. That limits assessment growth, while allowing local tax rates to rise. Walczak’s report concludes that the benefit of the lower assessment cap would be outweighed by the modeled tax shift.Supporters, including Florida Realtors, argue that homeowners also need help with housing costs.“Everywhere you look, people are feeling the pinch of affordability, and Amendment 3 has the opportunity to return more money back to the taxpayer,” said Margy Grant of Florida Realtors.The potential loss of local revenue has also drawn opposition from the Florida Sheriffs Association, which warns the amendment could squeeze funding for deputies and other public-safety needs.Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz pushed back against those warnings in a statement posted on X.“Tax relief and public safety are not competing priorities,” she said.Cordero-Stutz urged government agencies, including sheriffs’ offices, to examine their spending and eliminate unnecessary costs while protecting essential law-enforcement resources.Gov. Ron DeSantis supports Amendment 3 and says future lawmakers will pursue targeted state grants to help maintain essential services. He said the Legislature did not include the grant fund he sought in the amendment and that he plans to work with lawmakers on assistance.“We will ensure that essential services continue, but we also recognize taxpayers need a break,” DeSantis said.Florida voters will decide the measure Nov. The proposed constitutional amendment needs at least 60% of the votes cast on it to pass.

entry.article_text: When residents and visitors walk through downtown West Palm Beach, it's hard to miss the transformation.Construction cranes tower over city blocks, development projects are taking shape in nearly every direction and city leaders are trying to determine how future growth should unfold.WATCH BELOW: Downtown Master Plan: How West Palm residents can weigh in"A lot of growth happening. Just take a couple strolls down a few blocks and you'll see that there's construction going on everywhere," said Mark Alpaugh, who works downtown. "As a young professional like myself, it's exciting to see."For longtime residents and newcomers alike, the changing skyline is impossible to ignore."It's a completely different city," said downtown resident Gabriella Biondo, reflecting on the changes since she was a student at Palm Beach Atlantic University.The city Master Plan moved forward through the downtown action committee at the beginning of the month.And while many welcome the growth, city officials acknowledge it comes with challenges.Last week, the West Palm Beach Planning Board unanimously recommended approval of comprehensive plan amendments tied to the Downtown Master Plan update, a document that could help shape how downtown grows over the next several decades.The recommendation is not the final step. Additional public meetings and hearings are still planned before the City Commission makes final decisions.Throughout the discussion, city leaders and planning consultants repeatedly emphasized one key message:"Development is coming whether we like it or not," said consultant Bernard Zyscovich during the Downtown Master Plan presentation.Officials argued the city has two choices: proactively plan for growth or allow development to occur under existing regulations and state laws.Zyscovich said the city is trying to stay ahead of development pressures before they become more difficult to manage."There is no way to stop some of these things if we don't get ahead of it," Zyscovich said.Planning Board Chairman Steven Mayans said many of the issues residents are experiencing today are the result of West Palm Beach becoming a more desirable place to live."The problems are an outgrowth of success, and hopefully the growth is going to happen. Hopefully we're learning to manage it well," Mayans.One of the proposed changes centers on affordable housing.Under the plan, developers seeking additional building height and density would face stronger affordable housing requirements.Planning Director Anna Maria Ponte told board members:"The intention is to have every new project downtown basically support the construction of affordable housing," Ponte.The proposal would allow developers to build larger projects in certain districts, but only if they provide additional affordable housing or contribute toward affordable housing goals.For Biondo, that is one of the most important parts of the discussion.When asked what she hopes comes from the master plan, she said:"I would love less traffic, more affordable housing. All that sounds great," said Biondo. "It's not really affordable I would say to live downtown in West Palm Beach. I spend a lot of money for the convenience."City leaders also want to direct more development into transit-oriented areas near Brightline and Tri-Rail instead of pushing growth deeper into existing neighborhoods.Officials said those areas have stronger transportation options and are better suited to accommodate future development.The goal, they said, is to concentrate density where transit access is strongest while preserving the character of established neighborhoods.While affordable housing generated discussion, traffic remained the dominant concern throughout the meeting.City officials presented data showing Okeechobee Boulevard is operating at roughly 98% to 99% of planning capacity between Australian and Rosemary avenues.Residents and board members repeatedly raised concerns about congestion downtown and whether infrastructure can keep pace with new development.Alpaugh said traffic frustrations are already part of daily life."Okeechobee can sometimes get backed up, which can be frustrating," Alpaugh.One proposed solution would reduce the number of parking spaces developers are required to provide by about 25% in certain transit-oriented districts.Supporters argue fewer parking spaces could encourage greater use of public transportation, walking and biking.Planning Director Anna Maria Ponte defended the strategy during the meeting."If the concern is congestion, the solution is not to allow everybody to drive because we are never going to be able to have enough road for everybody," Ponte. "We're not restricting it. If you want to drive, you will be able to drive. We're not going to say you're not. But we offer other options for different alternatives and create certain friction. So the (best option is not always drive."Planning Board member Sam Fisch agreed saying, "The only way to have less traffic with more people is to have less cars."Several residents argued that future development isn't the biggest issue. Instead, they pointed to the impacts of projects already underway.Speakers described traffic detours, construction noise, dust, vibration and quality-of-life concerns.In response, city officials said they're evaluating stronger construction-management requirements, including regulations governing traffic plans, truck routes, staging areas, worker parking and enforcement measures.While many residents said they are not opposed to growth, several argued the city should move more carefully and ensure infrastructure can handle future development.One of the strongest comments came from resident Mark Hyman."Will it remain a livable city with a strong sense of community and an excellent quality of life? Growth is not the enemy, though. Poorly planned growth is."That statement captured much of the concern voiced by residents who say they want development but believe it must be managed carefully.The Planning Board's vote does not finalize the Downtown Master Plan.A public meeting is scheduled for Oct. 6 at Flagler Gallery at City Hall, followed by additional Planning Board discussions on Oct. City commissioners are expected to begin reviewing the plan later this fall.For now, the debate continues over how West Palm Beach should grow, and what kind of city it hopes to become in the years ahead.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead.

entry.title: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old student is facing a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat targeting Martin County High School Tuesday morning. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the student later admitted he made the threat because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. According to investigators, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL , a school safety reporting system, around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. During a news conference, Sheriff John Budensiek read the message that prompted the investigation. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," the sheriff read. The sheriff said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating. Authorities say surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. According to an affidavit, another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students. However, deputies said he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. According to Budensiek, Taylor later explained why he made the threat. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class." Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The arrest comes amid a string of bomb threats tied to Martin County High School. The sheriff said this is the fourth threat connected to the campus in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating, the sheriff added. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation. In a statement, Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact false threats can have on a school community. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek also warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences. "This individual has now been arrested, charged with a felony, getting expelled from school, likely. Getting a job down in the future is going to be very difficult for them because of the type of threat it is. These things that students think are funny can have long-term repercussions." The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

entry.title: Miami Dolphins open Hard Rock Stadium in week 3 against the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs
entry.summary: The Dolphins enter their home opener 0-2, having scored just 26 points while giving up 62 points per game in their first two games. The Miami Dolphins are preparing for their home opener at Hard Rock Stadium in week 3 of the NFL season, taking on the 2-0 Kansas City Chiefs. The Dolphins enter the matchup near the bottom of the league on both offense and defense. WATCH BELOW: Dolphins host undefeated Chiefs in Hard Rock home opener Dolphins look to rebound in home opener after 0-2 start Running back De'Von Achane said he is eager to play in front of the home crowd, even if the schedule pushed the opener to week 3. 'You always fired up when you go into Hard Rock. This year being our first home game in week three. Hopefully we don't get this schedule again,' Achane said. Head coach Jeff Hafley acknowledged the challenge the Chiefs present on both sides of the ball. 'Their o-line is solid and now you add one of the premier backs in this league who's currently leading the league in rushing, then you want to load the box and stop the runner. Then they have guys who can run by people, and they have a quarterback who can keep it alive,' Hafley said. That quarterback is Patrick Mahomes. Kenneth Walker III, one of the Chiefs' newest running backs, is already leading the league in rushing. Linebacker Jordyn Brooks said stopping Walker will be a priority. 'Got to tackle him man, he's breaking a bunch of tackles and very shifty can do it all,' Brooks said. In their first two games, the Dolphins scored just 26 points while giving up 62 points per game. Rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez said the team knows it must play better and that the fans deserve more. 'We got to play a lot better, and we got to give them something to cheer for. That starts with playing good defense. It's been a really frustrating two weeks, but that's on us, and we got to play better.' Kickoff is 1 p.m. Sunday at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens. entry.article_text: The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced on Tuesday, Sept. 22, that it arrested a 15-year-old Martin County High School student in connection with a false bomb threat made against the school. The sheriff’s office said its school resource officers and criminal investigations division traced the originator of the message back to the 15-year-old student, who is a sophomore at the school. WPBF 25 News is not publishing the name of the suspect because the student is under the age of 18 and has not been charged as an adult. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The sheriff’s office said the student confessed to sending the hoax threat. The student is facing a charge of false report concerning the planting of a bomb, which is a second-degree felony. “This arrest follows multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in our area over the past several weeks. Each threat is taken seriously and requires a significant response from law enforcement and emergency personnel, regardless of whether the threat ultimately proves to be a hoax,” the sheriff’s office said. It added that the suspect was only linked to the threat to the high school on Tuesday, Sept. “The Sheriff’s Office will thoroughly investigate these incidents and aggressively pursue those responsible when the investigation provides sufficient evidence to identify them. To anyone who thinks sending a threat anonymously, by text, online or through another form of electronic communication will automatically protect you from being identified and charged: that is not a safe assumption. These are not jokes, and will be treated as the crimes that they are.” Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back    WPEC
entry.article_text: Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a notice dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The notice says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the swale, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and numerous trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the swale, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. "It's just a little bit frustrating and disappointing that we, as homeowners, have to endure this from the HOA," said Keyla Peguero, a homeowner at Cadence at Tradition. Recently the HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees, at the homeowners' expense. But homeowners such as Chip Collison say the dead trees were in common areas, not their yards, so they want the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. "You think the swale is a common area?" we asked Collison. "Based on the documentation I've read? The notice sent to homeowners goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead. "We're well into hurricane season now. If we plant new trees, no one can predict the future. These trees could be freshly planted. We get a strong hurricane come through, they're all gone, and they're gonna have to be redone again," Collison said. Peguero says she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house, at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it with a new tree. She says she's not willing to do it again and shouldn't have had to do it in the first place. A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA sent us this written statement: Currently, the HOA is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in the common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. In the limited common areas, such as the rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons, residents are responsible for replacing trees and maintaining these areas. Because the HOA is currently purchasing and installing trees in bulk, we’ve invited residents to participate in the program. This allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring that tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally.

entry.summary: Man shot outside Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical now faces charges, police say    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 37-year-old man who was shot during a confrontation outside a Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie is now facing charges after investigators determined he was the primary aggressor in the encounter, according to police. Lucie Police Department said officers responded around 3:43 p.m. 19, to the restaurant at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard after receiving reports of a shooting. When officers arrived, they found Christopher Harris, 37, suffering from a gunshot wound to his upper torso. He was flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where his injuries were determined to be non-life-threatening, police said. The other person involved, identified by police as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while detectives investigated. Officers also recovered a firearm. According to investigators, the encounter began after Harris and Davis had an interaction in the restaurant's parking lot. Police said surveillance video showed Davis entering the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order and Harris following him inside, despite Harris not appearing to place or pick up an order. Police said Harris then followed Davis back outside, where exterior surveillance video showed Harris pushing Davis and advancing toward him as Davis moved backward. Investigators said Harris was armed with a knife during the confrontation, and witnesses reported seeing him with a knife shortly before the shooting. Davis fired one round, striking Harris in the chest, according to police. Harris went back inside the restaurant, where people began providing aid and called 911. Investigators said one knife was recovered after it had been removed from Harris' waistband while people were helping him. Police said another knife was later found in his front pocket. After reviewing surveillance video, physical evidence and witness statements, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor and established probable cause to charge him with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction, according to the department. Because Harris remained hospitalized, police said an arrest affidavit was submitted to the St. He is expected to be booked into the jail after he is medically released. Police said no criminal charges are currently pending against Davis. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates

entry.summary: A Jupiter mother who rallied her community to demand safer intersections on Military Trail is celebrating a major victory after Palm Beach County officials agreed to install new protected left-turn signals. The county confirmed the safety upgrades will be installed within three to four weeks at the intersections of Military Trail with both University Boulevard and Fredrick Small Road. The decision comes less than two weeks after WPTV first shared the story of Susan Tinsley , who began advocating for change after her husband witnessed the aftermath of a crash involving teenagers. entry.summary: Florida's two gubernatorial nominees offered sharply different visions for the state's economy Wednesday at the WLRN Sunshine Economy Summit in downtown Fort Lauderdale, where affordability, property taxes, and hurricane insurance dominated the conversation. Democrat David Jolly and Republican Byron Donalds spoke in back-to-back 30-minute panel discussions, but were kept separate throughout the event. Donalds said he supports the measure. 'I think voters need relief. I think the property owners need relief,' Donalds said. 'I anticipate I will vote against Amendment 3,' Jolly told the audience. 'I don't think the math works, and I think we know that because even Ron DeSantis now won't campaign for Amendment 3, and our sheriffs have come out and said, 'Please don't do this. It's going to defund services.'' Hurricane insurance Disaster relief and insurance costs also emerged as a major point of contrast. Jolly is proposing a sovereign wealth fund that would absorb hurricane and wind insurance burdens for Floridians. 'We are not going to solve this without government taking on a larger role in backing this. Otherwise, people are going to be priced out of their homes,' Jolly said. Donalds said that plan won't work. He is instead calling for the elimination of a premium surcharge that contributes to the state's catastrophic fund. 'We get through this hurricane season, the Cat Fund is estimated to have somewhere between 13 and 13-and-a-half billion dollars. entry.title: Crosswalk coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after safety study
entry.summary: A crosswalk is coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after a county pedestrian safety study confirmed it's needed. Palm Beach County Engineering and Public Works is working to agree on the exact location either at Haverhill and Carver or Haverhill and 4th before submitting the design to the City of Greenacres. Once the crosswalk is installed, a crossing guard will be placed there. WATCH BELOW: Crosswalk coming to Haverhill Road near this school Crosswalk coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after safety study The city tells WPTV's Christy Waite they will allocate for the crossing guard(s). Waite has been investigating safety conditions along Haverhill Road across from Greenacres Elementary School for nearly a month. Brandon and Lynn Pote are among the parents who raised concerns about the stretch of road. 'Right here on Haverhill there's no school zone and it's 40 mph,' Pote said. The City of Greenacres tells WPTV: iWe have been in touch with PBC and are happy to hear they conducted a study and will be moving forward with the crosswalk. Being Haverhill is a county road, the review and permitting will be solely done by Palm Beach County rather than here at the city. When referencing the city, it is possible they will send a design to us as a courtesy which would just be a quick administrative review/feedback. We did have discussion with Palm Beach County and agreed to allocate a crossing guard(s). As this is not a identified 'school zone' and may not include flashing beacons, we did request some type of flashers to increase visibility for the safety of the students and crossing guards. The city will not be financially responsible for the project other than the crossing guards/i. Waite reached out to the Palm Beach County School District about the area being a school zone. The district said in a statement: iGreenacres Elementary School resides in a school zone, where traffic speeds are limited to 20 miles per hour along Jackson Avenue during arrival and dismissal times. With school in session, we remind drivers to allow extra commute time and exercise caution near schools. Please remain highly alert for students, school buses, and heavier traffic./i The crosswalk is expected to be completed early next year. entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County
entry.summary: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. Woman who stole BSO patrol car found in ballistic vest in St. Lucie County, makes bizarre request to judge The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. WATCH BELOW: Shannon Marie Dillon makes her first appearance Fort Lauderdale woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's patrol car, abandoning it on I-95 At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m. Wednesday morning.

entry.title: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable - WPEC
entry.summary: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable    WPEC
entry.article_text: With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election.

entry.summary: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. See also: Can Florida police pull you over for a license plate frame? What the new law says Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie HOA tells residents to replace dead trees, homeowners push back    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a notice dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The notice says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the swale, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and numerous trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the swale, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. "It's just a little bit frustrating and disappointing that we, as homeowners, have to endure this from the HOA," said Keyla Peguero, a homeowner at Cadence at Tradition. Recently the HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees, at the homeowners' expense. But homeowners such as Chip Collison say the dead trees were in common areas, not their yards, so they want the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. "You think the swale is a common area?" we asked Collison. "Based on the documentation I've read? The notice sent to homeowners goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead. "We're well into hurricane season now. If we plant new trees, no one can predict the future. These trees could be freshly planted. We get a strong hurricane come through, they're all gone, and they're gonna have to be redone again," Collison said. Peguero says she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house, at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it with a new tree. She says she's not willing to do it again and shouldn't have had to do it in the first place. A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA sent us this written statement: Currently, the HOA is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in the common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. In the limited common areas, such as the rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons, residents are responsible for replacing trees and maintaining these areas. Because the HOA is currently purchasing and installing trees in bulk, we’ve invited residents to participate in the program. This allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring that tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally.

entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - WPBF
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. entry.title: Father pulls gun on teens at Indiantown bus stop, NAACP calls for action - WPBF
entry.summary: Father pulls gun on teens at Indiantown bus stop, NAACP calls for action    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation at a school bus stop in Indiantown, where a father pulled a gun on two teenagers after his son reported being bullied, has sparked community discussions and involvement from the NAACP. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said the incident began last Thursday when the man’s son reported being bullied. The next day, the father went to the bus stop to drop off his son and started speaking with the bus driver. According to the sheriff, two students then left the bus and confronted the father. “The dad's got his hand up, telling them to stay back, stay back, stay back,” said Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. The sheriff explained that the father pulled out a concealed weapon when the teens approached him. “They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do. He's legally allowed to stand his ground,” Budensiek said. The two students involved, Trevor Ivory and RJ McIntyre, shared their perspective on the incident. “I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school,” Ivory said. “Instead, they had to see a man with a gun on two teenagers that they know ride the bus in the morning.” The confrontation was a key topic during an NAACP community meeting held Tuesday night. The two students and their families attended the meeting, where emotions ran high. “The dad had a thousand options. He chose the wrong option,” said Pam Ivory, Trevor’s aunt. Jimmy Smith, president of the NAACP Martin County Branch, also addressed the situation. “We know guns aren’t allowed on school property. They also shouldn’t be allowed in school bus stops,” Smith said. Smith added that he plans to meet with the school board and the sheriff to discuss the incident further. “We shouldn’t be pointing a gun at our children,” he said. The sheriff’s office stated that it conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had chosen to press charges. However, no arrests have been made, and the sheriff reiterated that the father acted within the law. entry.title: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say - cw34.com
entry.summary: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old student is facing a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat targeting Martin County High School Tuesday morning. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the student later admitted he made the threat because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. According to investigators, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL , a school safety reporting system, around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. During a news conference, Sheriff John Budensiek read the message that prompted the investigation. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," the sheriff read. The sheriff said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating. Authorities say surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. According to an affidavit, another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students. However, deputies said he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. According to Budensiek, Taylor later explained why he made the threat. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class." Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The arrest comes amid a string of bomb threats tied to Martin County High School. The sheriff said this is the fourth threat connected to the campus in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating, the sheriff added. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation. In a statement, Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact false threats can have on a school community. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek also warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences. "This individual has now been arrested, charged with a felony, getting expelled from school, likely. Getting a job down in the future is going to be very difficult for them because of the type of threat it is. These things that students think are funny can have long-term repercussions." The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

entry.summary: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. See also: Can Florida police pull you over for a license plate frame? What the new law says Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

entry.title: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable - WPEC
entry.summary: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable    WPEC
entry.article_text: With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election.

entry.summary: Martin County High student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half. WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threat The arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks. Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus. When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement. "Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip." However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff.
