entry.article_text: Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie property tax rate going downSince 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

entry.article_text: Prediction site Polymarket rolled out new consumer protections and anti-addiction measures Wednesday, as a growing number of policymakers call for more regulation of the booming industry.Prediction sites have exploded in popularity this year, with billions of dollars wagered on everything from sports to elections, entertainment and even the weather.Polymarket will now allow users to create deposit limits that can’t be immediately undone, so they can slow down their spending and potential losses. Users can also place themselves on an “exclusion list” that would temporarily or permanently block them from the platform.The company is also offering new access to mental health resources for users exhibiting what it calls “compulsive financial trading behaviors.” This is part of a new partnership with Birches Health, a virtual gambling addiction therapy company.“Right now, the number-one priority is just getting this out, giving it into the hands of the millions of people that leverage and use us, and trust us to protect them and keep them safe,” Malea Otranto, Polymarket’s new head of global safety, told CNN in an interview.Prediction sites are similar to gambling in terms of risking real money, but they’re legally classified as federally regulated financial markets, which means they don’t have to follow state consumer protection laws for casinos and sportsbooks. It falls on companies to voluntarily offer tools that users can opt into – which many state and federal lawmakers say is inadequate.RELATED STORY | States can regulate prediction markets as gambling, federal appeals court rulesJonathan Cohen, who leads gambling policy at the American Institute for Boys and Men, praised these moves but said their impact may be limited, pointing to data from state regulators showing that few gamblers utilize similar tools on sportsbooks.“These restrictions are standard fare for online sports-betting platforms,” Cohen said. “The companies are clearly recognizing that from a user standpoint, the behavior is similar to, if not synonymous with, gambling.”Asked about the effectiveness of these “responsible trading” tools, Otranto said Polymarket will be tracking usage of these tools and might make adjustments in the future.“It’s really incredibly important as we continue to grow and accelerate to give people control over how they want to leverage our platform,” Otranto said.Promoting ‘responsible trading’Prediction sites like Polymarket and Kalshi are regulated federally by the CFTC, a small federal agency that has historically spent most of its time policing commodities trading, like soybean futures and oil derivatives.But sports markets are the main drivers of the prediction frenzy. Sports and multi-leg parlays popular with sports made up more than 98% of trading volume this month on Polymarket’s US site, according to TickerTracker, a data analysis firm.This is part of the reason why “responsible trading” safeguards on Polymarket and Kalshi resemble the “responsible gaming” policies at sportsbooks like DraftKings and FanDuel.Polymarket’s deputy chief legal officer Olivia Chalos acknowledged these similarities, but said the company follows a different business model than sportsbooks, and wants to protect users, especially younger users, who aren’t experienced with financial exchanges.“You’re seeing a user base that did not previously participate in financial markets coming in, and doing this at scale,” Chalos told CNN. “With that, there are measures that need to be in place, because you’re recognizing an audience that is participating in markets for the first time.”State vs. federal regulationGaming lawyer Joshua Kirschner said “there is no analogue” in existing federal law that gets close to matching the seemingly “endless list of various tools” found in state regulations that require casinos and sportsbooks to promote responsible gambling and to combat gambling addiction.That’s one reason why a bipartisan coalition of 44 states have argued in court that prediction platforms should be subjected to state laws and regulated like gambling.Polymarket’s announcement comes one week after New York filed a lawsuit seeking to shut down the company.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | New York sues prediction market platform Kalshi, alleging 'illegal gambling operation'State investigators said Polymarket is circumventing New York’s “strict regulation of licensed gambling,” which includes requirements to block underage users, rules against predatory advertising, mandatory funding for addiction programs, and “self-exclusion” policies.Polymarket denies wrongdoing and filed a countersuit against New York in federal court. The state is also suing Kalshi, which said the case is baseless and will “hurt New Yorkers.”“These protections are good for consumers,” Kirschner said of Polymarket’s new safety measures, “but maybe it’s also a nod to try to pacify state regulators.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

entry.title: Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo go one-on-one during first day of Miami Heat training camp
entry.summary: The Miami Heat are on the court. The team held day one of training camp on Tuesday at Florida Atlantic University. Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo went one-on-one during camp, with the former best defensive player in the league challenging the most versatile defender the Heat has ever seen. WATCH BELOW: Bam, Giannis take the court as Heat training camp begins Miami Heat training camp underway at FAU Head coach Erik Spoelstra said he welcomes that competitive energy between the two. 'I want that competitive spirit when they are going at each other,' Spoelstra said. But Spoelstra said getting the two stars playing together is just as important as the individual competition. 'We also need to get them on the same page, playing together. I want to get those reps, in this preseason,' Spoelstra said. That includes reps on defense, where the Adebayo-Antetokounmpo pairing could create serious problems for opposing offenses. 'We noticed that the last three, two, three, four years that teams were scheming against Bam's defense. Just like you have to scheme against Giannis' defense. Now we have two guys that can do both things. Hopefully that will really help I'll make our defense more dynamic,' Spoelstra said. Spoelstra said having both players on the floor at the same time opens up more opportunities defensively. 'It'll allow them each to make more plays, defensive plays in the paint, blocks, deflections, stops,' Spoelstra said. Adebayo and Antetokounmpo both said they plan to push each other in practice to elevate the team's defense. 'We're a fast team, but not only are we fast, we're switchable, we talk, we communicate, everybody can guard their yard. And that's one through five and from that standpoint, I feel like we're going to be really good.' Adebayo said. 'Because the defense is mindset and effort and I feel like we have guys around the team that have that,' Antetokounmpo said. On the offensive end, players including Davion Mitchell, Pelle Larsson and Klay Thompson got in plenty of shots during practice. Spoelstra said this year the team is turning the page and starting something new. The Heat will continue to practice at Florida Atlantic University throughout the week before heading to Toronto to face the Raptors in a preseason game Saturday.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie removes 18 Flock cameras as privacy concerns grow - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie removes 18 Flock cameras as privacy concerns grow    WPBF
entry.article_text: Florida's deadline to remove Flock cameras from highway rights-of-way is Wednesday, Sept. Lucie is also removing 18 cameras from city streets after pausing its program due to privacy concerns. Florida’s Department of Transportation mandated that local agencies remove Flock cameras from state highway rights-of-way by today. These cameras capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to investigate crimes. However, the state order does not apply to cameras on city streets or county roads, leaving local governments to set their own rules. Lucie, the city commission voted to have the vendor remove 18 cameras today after pausing its Flock program. During Monday’s city commission meeting, one resident said, "Mass surveillance is wrong and has a negative impact on those under that surveillance. We have become too comfortable with bleeding-edge technologies without proper research or testing." Critics have raised concerns about how the cameras store the data and who can access it. Flock, the company behind the cameras, said the agency using the system controls the data, not Flock. The company also said that data is deleted by default after 30 days and that every search is logged, including details about who conducted the search, why, and when. Another resident urged the city to take broader action, saying, "I'm asking you to remove the city's Flock cameras and take broader action in St. Lucie County has taken in its rights-of-way." While the state’s order applies only to cameras on state highways, Port St. Lucie is taking its own steps by removing the 18 cameras from city streets. The city’s decision reflects ongoing concerns about privacy and surveillance technology. entry.title: Fact check: Donalds ad claims Jolly's hurricane insurance plan would cost Florida families $1,000 per year
entry.summary: With less than five weeks until Election Day, a campaign ad from Republican Byron Donalds claims Democrat David Jolly's hurricane insurance proposal would cost Florida families $1,000 a year in what the ad calls a 'hurricane tax.' An examination of the ad and the study it cites tells a more complicated story. The Donalds ad's claims The ad opens by asking, 'How much will David Jolly's hurricane tax cost Florida?' and cites a Florida State University study to support its assertion that Jolly's plan would run Florida families $1,000 per year. 'A giant bail-out for big insurance. A giant rip-off for you,' the 30-second spot says. RELATED: More political, election news What Jolly is proposing Jolly wants to create what he calls a 'sovereign wealth fund' to absorb all windstorm coverage in Florida, while allowing private insurers to handle other types of policies. When I asked him at an event in Fort Lauderdale recently to explain the concept, Jolly pushed back on the 'hurricane tax' framing. 'Well, there's currently a thousand-dollar hurricane tax on the books that Byron Donalds wants to continue. My model would actually repeal it,' Jolly said. What's actually on the books Florida does not have a specific 'hurricane tax' on the books. Jolly is likely referring to the assessments that Citizens Property Insurance is required to levy on Floridians in order to remain solvent. Jolly's campaign claims that if private insurers don't have to worry about windstorm policies, premiums would drop 60 to 70 percent. I was not able to independently verify that math. 'A state sovereign wealth fund can absorb the risk of hurricane coverage if we sufficiently capitalize it,' Jolly said. What the cited FSU study actually says The Donalds ad cites a Florida State University study which I obtained via a public records request. It was commissioned by the policy research arm of the Florida Legislature and released in August. The 80-page report does not examine Jolly's specific proposal of a sovereign wealth fund. Instead, it looks into the feasibility of having Citizens Property Insurance bear all the risk for named windstorms, taking the burden off private insurers. The report says that proposal could under some circumstances lower premiums. But it would ultimately redistribute the risk from Florida's most hurricane-prone areas and spread it across the state, 'effectively (creating) a broader 'hurricane tax...'' by '(increasing) the likelihood and magnitude of statewide assessments

When asked how the investigation might have unfolded without the technology, Araujo said things would have turned out differently."I've been a cop for 45 years. We'd probably still be looking for the suspect," he said.Araujo credited dispatchers, officers, investigators, and professional staff across multiple units, including patrol, criminal investigations, the real-time crime center, and the crime scene unit, for their work across multiple crime scenes.He also thanked State Attorney Alexcia Cox's office for assistance with numerous search warrants and the arrest warrant, as well as the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and the Broward County Sheriff's Office.Milner faces charges of first-degree murder with a firearm, attempted first-degree murder with a firearm, and shooting into an occupied vehicle. entry.title: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route    WPEC
entry.article_text: A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. Jim Harvey, president of Brookfield Kolter Land Partners, declined to comment on the request. We have no comment at this time, Harvey said in an email to CBS12 News. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place, Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county’s existing growth plan. Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what’s going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that’s wrong, Braun said. Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing, Smart said. People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that. Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there’s a lot of moving parts, Knobbe said. The property is outside the county’s urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements. I think the effect is going to be more traffic. I think the effect is going to be more sprawl. I think the effect is going to be municipal services overextended, Smart said. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie lowers property tax rate for 11th straight year - WPTV
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie lowers property tax rate for 11th straight year    WPTV
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie property tax rate going downSince 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

entry.title: Decision not to charge parent in Indiantown bus stop gun incident sparks heated community debate - wflx.com
entry.summary: Decision not to charge parent in Indiantown bus stop gun incident sparks heated community debate    wflx.com
entry.article_text: Outrage and frustration boiled over at a community meeting in Indiantown, as residents packed a room to demand answers from the Martin County Sheriff's Office after a parent who pulled a gun on two students at a bus stop was not charged with a crime. The tense Monday night meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and the sheriff, centered on the sheriff's determination that the father acted in self-defense. However, many residents argued that the man should have been arrested for the separate crime of possessing a firearm at a school bus stop. WATCH BELOW: Indiantown divided over bus stop gun incident, no-charge decision Sheriff John Budensiek laid out his office's account of the incident, which occurred just over a week ago. He said it began with a student being bullied and struck by another student on a school bus. The victim's father went to the bus stop to report the bullying to the driver. The situation escalated, Budensiek said, when the alleged bully and a friend "pushed past the bus driver and tried to confront the dad." "He puts his hand up and backs up, backs up, says 'stay away, stay away,' and they don't," Budensiek explained. "In fact, they’re yelling that they’re going to whoop his hind end... He pulls out a gun and all of a sudden they’re backing up, because they don’t want to get shot." The sheriff defended the lack of charges against the father, citing the state's self-defense laws. "In the state of Florida, you’re allowed to defend yourself against someone coming after you," he said. But residents at the meeting were furious, arguing that the father was committing a misdemeanor by possessing a gun at a bus stop, which they believe should negate his "Stand Your Ground" defense. "Stand Your Ground cannot come into play because at the time you were committing a crime by being at that bus stop with a gun," one resident yelled. The sheriff countered that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a "bus stop," making that specific charge unenforceable in this case. The father also declined to press battery charges against the two students. Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to channel their anger toward changing those laws. "These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket." He said that while there was disagreement, everyone shared one sentiment: "We can agree that this should have never happened." entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested after police said he called 911 and admitted to stabbing a 79-year-old man during a domestic-related incident Saturday night. Police said Cartavion Jermaine Merritt called 911 about 11:01 p.m. to report a stabbing inside a home in the 11200 block of Northwest Blockbird Drive. Lucie police, Merritt told dispatchers he used two knives to stab the victim in the chest and wanted to kill him. He also told dispatchers the two men were the only people inside the home and that he had put the knives in the kitchen sink. Body-camera video released by police shows officers arriving in the neighborhood, establishing a perimeter and escorting a man away from the home. Police said Merritt exited the house about eight minutes after the 911 call and was taken into custody without incident. Once officers entered, they found the 79-year-old victim with multiple apparent stab wounds to his upper chest, police said. Officers and paramedics provided emergency care before the victim was flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital as a trauma alert. See also: Airport security concerns resurface after perimeter breaches in South Florida The victim was later reported stable but intubated, police said. Investigators said they found two knives in the kitchen sink and blood on bedsheets in a bedroom, where they determined the stabbing occurred. Police said Merritt later told detectives that he intended to kill the victim. Merritt was arrested on charges of attempted second-degree murder without premeditation and aggravated battery on a person 65 or older, both domestic-related charges.

P1 Motor Club expects to welcome members onto its first racetrack within a month, offering an early taste of a community where owners will eventually be able to drive on a circuit and head home overlooking it. The 650-acre development on Okeechobee Road is taking shape on a former orange grove. Plans include multiple driving circuits, trackside homes, a motorsports business park and amenities ranging from a pool to walking trails. The easiest way to describe it that most people understand is think of a high-end golf club, but a racetrack, said Chris Duplessis, P1’s director of fun. So no golf balls, we’ve got fancy race cars instead. CBS12 News took a ride with Duplessis for a firsthand look at the three-mile track, which he said is about 85% complete. Remaining work includes finishing sections of guardrail while the newly laid asphalt cures. Construction on what visitors see today started about a year ago, following several years of planning and approvals, he said. See also: Citadel CEO's historic $3 billion gift is bringing Carnegie Mellon to Miami Eventually, the property will have just under 10 miles of driving surfaces. A planned 4.5-mile circuit will include elevation changes and a crossover bridge where the track passes over itself. Other plans include karting, rally and drifting areas. Duplessis said construction on the larger circuit and real estate portion is expected to begin around the start of 2027. P1 plans to pay for a water line connecting the development to county water service. Homes with a view of the action For some members, P1 will be a place to spend the day. For others, it will become a home or weekend getaway. Duplessis said the club already has 280 members and has sold 68 real estate units. The planned garage townhomes will combine ground-floor vehicle space with living areas upstairs. Each unit will overlook a track, he said. These are fully livable, garage on the ground level, beautiful living space upstairs, Duplessis said. Every unit is overlooking the track, so they all have track view as well as community view. P1 also plans trackside residences. Duplessis estimated the development will eventually include roughly 200 residential units, with many buyers expected to use them as second or third homes. Only members can purchase real estate. Membership currently starts at $192,000, with yearly dues in addition. Duplessis quoted real estate at $1.4 million, purchased separately. Residents could begin moving in in about two years, he said. The full development is expected to take approximately five years to complete. A fleet of cars and coaching for beginners Members will not necessarily need to bring their own car to get behind the wheel. Duplessis said P1’s partnership with Mercedes will provide a fleet of vehicles for members to drive. He also described plans for Mercedes-hosted driving experiences that would give nonmembers opportunities to use the track. While luxury cars are part of the appeal, Duplessis said the vehicles on the circuit could range from Mazda Miatas to Porsches, Ferraris and Mercedes models. Some members have racing experience. Others have never driven on a track. For beginners, P1 plans to provide instructors who teach driving fundamentals and track rules before building toward more advanced skills. We get them an instructor, an expert, teach them all the basics, all the rules of the road, let’s say, and then they start driving, Duplessis said. The circuit has no posted speed limit, but drivers will be expected to stay within their abilities. New drivers will work with coaches who control the pace as they learn. Members whose skills qualify them will also have opportunities to participate in club races. Beyond the racetrack The development’s plans include a clubhouse, pool, pickleball and other sport courts, lakes and walking trails. Duplessis said a rooftop bar at the clubhouse will offer views of the activity below. He said the team is also considering nature as it lays out the property, including pond locations intended to support bird life. An area with mature trees is planned for slower, technical off-road driving. The team is exploring water sports on the property’s lakes, though those activities are still being considered. P1 also plans space for motorsports-related businesses. Duplessis said the club intends to host community events where nonmembers can visit and watch, along with driving training for law enforcement. He said local workers and contractors are already involved in the project. For Duplessis, a four-time national rally champion, the development is personal. He plans to make it his home. I will live right here, he said. It’ll be a big sense of community for all our members. Duplessis said P1 will bring jobs and use local contractors and businesses, noting a track he previously ran employed about 150 people; he did not provide a hiring estimate for P1. He expects little traffic impact, saying many homes will be used only occasionally and a busy day would draw about 100 members.

entry.article_text: Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. "To me, that is absolutely ludicrous. There's no way that that should happen in this community. So I'm very upset that that is in our neighborhood," said Gail Lucas, a neighbor. Lucas said she has seen three children at the house. She said she was saddened that police found drugs in the home where there were kids. It's just, oh, it gives me the creeps," Lucas said. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. "I'm glad that they did, you know, take care of that," Lucas said after she learned Francis has been arrested. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

entry.title: Dolphins RB De'Von Achane maintaining positive attitude after season-ending ACL tear, Hafley says
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins confirmed earlier this week that running back De'Von Achane tore his ACL on Sunday and will miss the rest of the season. Achane was injured just five plays into Sunday's game against the Kansas City Chiefs , leaving the game after an uncomfortable tackle. Head coach Jeff Hafley said Wednesday that Achane has maintained a positive attitude but acknowledged the road ahead will not be easy. 'As far as how he's doing, he's had a great attitude. I'm sure he's going to have some tough moments,' Hafley said. 'There's going to be some really hard days and then there'll be some days where he's this positive, energetic self,' Hafley said. Hafley said the recovery goes beyond the physical. 'Whenever you go through a serious injury, it's not just a physical recovery; it's mental. We got to make sure that he's doing OK, and that's very important to me,' Hafley said. Without their star running back, the Dolphins are preparing for Week 4 against the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings. So far this season, Miami has faced opponents that are all 3-0. Hafley said the team is focused on taking things one week at a time. 'Each week we just try to go 1-0 and not look ahead or behind. But we know we've played really good teams. And I think individually we went up against a lot of really good players. And I think we're gaining experience and we're getting better because of that,' Hafley said. This week is no different, as the Dolphins hit the road again to face the undefeated Vikings. 'To get a chance to go there, and I think one of the better atmospheres in the NFL with a really good team and a really good staff, I think it's a huge challenge. But I think they've embraced it. I know they have. I think we've all embraced it,' Hafley said. The Dolphins will look to secure their first win of the season Sunday. Kickoff is at 4:05 p.m. Eastern.

The child was playing outside in the yard along Darling Street with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he slipped out of sight for a brief period. Family members told investigators the child was out of their sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone present at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances surrounding the tragedy. The investigation remains ongoing.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie removes 18 Flock cameras as privacy concerns grow    WPBF
entry.article_text: Florida's deadline to remove Flock cameras from highway rights-of-way is Wednesday, Sept. Lucie is also removing 18 cameras from city streets after pausing its program due to privacy concerns. Florida’s Department of Transportation mandated that local agencies remove Flock cameras from state highway rights-of-way by today. These cameras capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to investigate crimes. However, the state order does not apply to cameras on city streets or county roads, leaving local governments to set their own rules. Lucie, the city commission voted to have the vendor remove 18 cameras today after pausing its Flock program. During Monday’s city commission meeting, one resident said, "Mass surveillance is wrong and has a negative impact on those under that surveillance. We have become too comfortable with bleeding-edge technologies without proper research or testing." Critics have raised concerns about how the cameras store the data and who can access it. Flock, the company behind the cameras, said the agency using the system controls the data, not Flock. The company also said that data is deleted by default after 30 days and that every search is logged, including details about who conducted the search, why, and when. Another resident urged the city to take broader action, saying, "I'm asking you to remove the city's Flock cameras and take broader action in St. Lucie County has taken in its rights-of-way." While the state’s order applies only to cameras on state highways, Port St. Lucie is taking its own steps by removing the 18 cameras from city streets. The city’s decision reflects ongoing concerns about privacy and surveillance technology. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," adding he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Per Sabol's resignation, Lee said it's a "sad day." "She's been a tremendous attorney for the district," Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over with "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee told Hussey. "I came up on the labor side, I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday's meeting."This system is so broken," one attendee said."Everybody is fed up. They want action," said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins.As the union's legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, "I think we might actually," adding, "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I'm going to ask the board in a week from now — what do we want to do? What's the process?" Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote. entry.title: Fact check: Donalds ad claims Jolly's hurricane insurance plan would cost Florida families $1,000 per year
entry.summary: With less than five weeks until Election Day, a campaign ad from Republican Byron Donalds claims Democrat David Jolly's hurricane insurance proposal would cost Florida families $1,000 a year in what the ad calls a 'hurricane tax.' An examination of the ad and the study it cites tells a more complicated story. The Donalds ad's claims The ad opens by asking, 'How much will David Jolly's hurricane tax cost Florida?' and cites a Florida State University study to support its assertion that Jolly's plan would run Florida families $1,000 per year. 'A giant bail-out for big insurance. A giant rip-off for you,' the 30-second spot says. RELATED: More political, election news What Jolly is proposing Jolly wants to create what he calls a 'sovereign wealth fund' to absorb all windstorm coverage in Florida, while allowing private insurers to handle other types of policies. When I asked him at an event in Fort Lauderdale recently to explain the concept, Jolly pushed back on the 'hurricane tax' framing. 'Well, there's currently a thousand-dollar hurricane tax on the books that Byron Donalds wants to continue. My model would actually repeal it,' Jolly said. What's actually on the books Florida does not have a specific 'hurricane tax' on the books. Jolly is likely referring to the assessments that Citizens Property Insurance is required to levy on Floridians in order to remain solvent. Jolly's campaign claims that if private insurers don't have to worry about windstorm policies, premiums would drop 60 to 70 percent. I was not able to independently verify that math. 'A state sovereign wealth fund can absorb the risk of hurricane coverage if we sufficiently capitalize it,' Jolly said. What the cited FSU study actually says The Donalds ad cites a Florida State University study which I obtained via a public records request. It was commissioned by the policy research arm of the Florida Legislature and released in August. The 80-page report does not examine Jolly's specific proposal of a sovereign wealth fund. Instead, it looks into the feasibility of having Citizens Property Insurance bear all the risk for named windstorms, taking the burden off private insurers. The report says that proposal could under some circumstances lower premiums. Instead, it looks into the feasibility of having Citizens Property Insurance bear all the risk for named windstorms, taking the burden off private insurers.The report says that proposal could — under some circumstances — lower premiums. But it would ultimately redistribute the risk from Florida's most hurricane-prone areas and spread it across the state, "effectively (creating) a broader 'hurricane tax...'" by "(increasing) the likelihood and magnitude of statewide assessments."Read the full study below:How Jolly would fund the sovereign wealth fundI followed up with Jolly, asking how he would get the money for the sovereign wealth fund, which he says would need at least $32 million to start."So let's start with the existing hurricane fund, the $12 billion in the current fee structure," Jolly said. "(And) if we require our insurance companies to actually keep their profits in state instead of shipping them out of state, you could raise several billion dollars a year doing that as well. I've also mentioned looking at a tourist development tax."Jolly also suggested starting with partial windstorm coverage from the fund, then rolling out full coverage as it grows over time.Donalds pushes backDonalds says his opponent's math still doesn't add up."When it comes to insurance company profits, he says he wants to tax, if you take 70% of their business away from them, what profits are you taxing?" Donalds said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Race, then head home: Inside St. Lucie County’s P1 Motor Club - cw34.com
entry.summary: Race, then head home: Inside St. Lucie County’s P1 Motor Club    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The 650-acre development plans nearly 10 miles of driving surfaces, trackside homes and country club amenities. Membership currently starts at $192,000. P1 Motor Club expects to welcome members onto its first racetrack within a month, offering an early taste of a community where owners will eventually be able to drive on a circuit and head home overlooking it. The 650-acre development on Okeechobee Road is taking shape on a former orange grove. Plans include multiple driving circuits, trackside homes, a motorsports business park and amenities ranging from a pool to walking trails. The easiest way to describe it that most people understand is think of a high-end golf club, but a racetrack, said Chris Duplessis, P1’s director of fun. So no golf balls, we’ve got fancy race cars instead. CBS12 News took a ride with Duplessis for a firsthand look at the three-mile track, which he said is about 85% complete. Remaining work includes finishing sections of guardrail while the newly laid asphalt cures. Construction on what visitors see today started about a year ago, following several years of planning and approvals, he said. See also: Citadel CEO's historic $3 billion gift is bringing Carnegie Mellon to Miami Eventually, the property will have just under 10 miles of driving surfaces. A planned 4.5-mile circuit will include elevation changes and a crossover bridge where the track passes over itself. Other plans include karting, rally and drifting areas. Duplessis said construction on the larger circuit and real estate portion is expected to begin around the start of 2027. P1 plans to pay for a water line connecting the development to county water service. Homes with a view of the action For some members, P1 will be a place to spend the day. For others, it will become a home or weekend getaway. Duplessis said the club already has 280 members and has sold 68 real estate units. The planned garage townhomes will combine ground-floor vehicle space with living areas upstairs. Each unit will overlook a track, he said. These are fully livable, garage on the ground level, beautiful living space upstairs, Duplessis said. Every unit is overlooking the track, so they all have track view as well as community view. P1 also plans trackside residences. Duplessis estimated the development will eventually include roughly 200 residential units, with many buyers expected to use them as second or third homes. Only members can purchase real estate. Membership currently starts at $192,000, with yearly dues in addition. Duplessis quoted real estate at $1.4 million, purchased separately. Residents could begin moving in in about two years, he said. The full development is expected to take approximately five years to complete. A fleet of cars and coaching for beginners Members will not necessarily need to bring their own car to get behind the wheel. Duplessis said P1’s partnership with Mercedes will provide a fleet of vehicles for members to drive. He also described plans for Mercedes-hosted driving experiences that would give nonmembers opportunities to use the track. While luxury cars are part of the appeal, Duplessis said the vehicles on the circuit could range from Mazda Miatas to Porsches, Ferraris and Mercedes models. Some members have racing experience. Others have never driven on a track. For beginners, P1 plans to provide instructors who teach driving fundamentals and track rules before building toward more advanced skills. We get them an instructor, an expert, teach them all the basics, all the rules of the road, let’s say, and then they start driving, Duplessis said. The circuit has no posted speed limit, but drivers will be expected to stay within their abilities. New drivers will work with coaches who control the pace as they learn. Members whose skills qualify them will also have opportunities to participate in club races. Beyond the racetrack The development’s plans include a clubhouse, pool, pickleball and other sport courts, lakes and walking trails. Duplessis said a rooftop bar at the clubhouse will offer views of the activity below. He said the team is also considering nature as it lays out the property, including pond locations intended to support bird life. An area with mature trees is planned for slower, technical off-road driving. The team is exploring water sports on the property’s lakes, though those activities are still being considered. P1 also plans space for motorsports-related businesses. Duplessis said the club intends to host community events where nonmembers can visit and watch, along with driving training for law enforcement. He said local workers and contractors are already involved in the project. For Duplessis, a four-time national rally champion, the development is personal. He plans to make it his home. I will live right here, he said. It’ll be a big sense of community for all our members. Duplessis said P1 will bring jobs and use local contractors and businesses, noting a track he previously ran employed about 150 people; he did not provide a hiring estimate for P1. He expects little traffic impact, saying many homes will be used only occasionally and a busy day would draw about 100 members.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. "To me, that is absolutely ludicrous. There's no way that that should happen in this community. So I'm very upset that that is in our neighborhood," said Gail Lucas, a neighbor. Lucas said she has seen three children at the house. She said she was saddened that police found drugs in the home where there were kids. It's just, oh, it gives me the creeps," Lucas said. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. "I'm glad that they did, you know, take care of that," Lucas said after she learned Francis has been arrested. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie removes 18 Flock cameras as privacy concerns grow - wpbf.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie removes 18 Flock cameras as privacy concerns grow    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: Florida's deadline to remove Flock cameras from highway rights-of-way is Wednesday, Sept. Lucie is also removing 18 cameras from city streets after pausing its program due to privacy concerns. Florida’s Department of Transportation mandated that local agencies remove Flock cameras from state highway rights-of-way by today. These cameras capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to investigate crimes. However, the state order does not apply to cameras on city streets or county roads, leaving local governments to set their own rules. Lucie, the city commission voted to have the vendor remove 18 cameras today after pausing its Flock program. During Monday’s city commission meeting, one resident said, "Mass surveillance is wrong and has a negative impact on those under that surveillance. We have become too comfortable with bleeding-edge technologies without proper research or testing." Critics have raised concerns about how the cameras store the data and who can access it. Flock, the company behind the cameras, said the agency using the system controls the data, not Flock. The company also said that data is deleted by default after 30 days and that every search is logged, including details about who conducted the search, why, and when. Another resident urged the city to take broader action, saying, "I'm asking you to remove the city's Flock cameras and take broader action in St. Lucie County has taken in its rights-of-way." While the state’s order applies only to cameras on state highways, Port St. Lucie is taking its own steps by removing the 18 cameras from city streets. The city’s decision reflects ongoing concerns about privacy and surveillance technology.
